parts.name: Amiad 25 mm compact screen filter (130 micron)
parts.protocol_settings: 25 mm BSP in/out. 130 micron stainless screen. Flush the element, do not run it to blockage.
parts.evidence: Fitted upstream of every dripline zone in this fleet. Counted against the zone-valve nodes it protects; like the transformer it is plumbing rather than a configured device, so it does not appear in any YAML.
failure_modes: Left unflushed it blocks, pressure drops, and the far end of the dripline silently under-waters - the plants tell you before any sensor does.
130 micron passes fine silt that will still clog PCJ drippers over a season; go to 120 mesh / 100 micron if your source water is dirty.
The plastic body will crack if over-tightened onto a rigid PVC riser - use a union.
No differential-pressure indicator on the compact models, so blockage is invisible until flow drops.
parts.notes: The cheapest insurance in the whole irrigation stack. A NZ$49 filter protects a few hundred dollars of drippers and, more importantly, stops the uneven watering that partial blockage causes - which is far harder to diagnose than an outright failure. Fit it upstream of the solenoids, not downstream.

parts.name: AS7341 11-channel spectral sensor

i2c.how_to_change: Fixed at 0x39. Two on one bus needs a mux.

parts.calibration_notes: Gives you eight visible bands plus NIR and clear, but raw counts are gain- and integration-time dependent. To compare two rooms you must fix gain/ATIME/ASTEP and normalise against a reference measurement - otherwise the numbers only mean something relative to themselves.
parts.evidence: Listed in the facility spec as the second flower room light instrument (PPFD/DLI) alongside BH1750, but no current ESPHome device config carries an active AS7341 block - so it is documented as 'works', not field-proven, on this evidence.
failure_modes: Raw channel counts are meaningless without pinning gain and integration time first - change either and every number shifts.
Saturates fast directly under a modern LED bar; drop the gain or diffuse the window.
The NIR and clear channels pick up far-red supplemental strips, which can look like a spectrum shift that is not there.
Fixed 0x39 address, so multi-point spectral logging needs a mux.
parts.notes: The interesting use in a grow room is spectrum drift over a fixture's life and verifying far-red / UV supplement timing, not absolute PPFD. Pair with a real quantum sensor for absolute numbers.

example.title: AS7341 with gain and integration pinned
example.source: reference config - not currently deployed in this fleet
example.code:
i2c:
  sda: GPIO16
  scl: GPIO17

sensor:
  - platform: as7341
    address: 0x39
    update_interval: 60s
    # Pin gain/ATIME/ASTEP and NEVER change them if you want the channel
    # counts to stay comparable between rooms or across a fixture's life.
    gain: X8
    atime: 100
    astep: 999
    f1: { name: "415nm violet" }
    f4: { name: "515nm green" }
    f6: { name: "630nm red" }
    f8: { name: "680nm deep red" }
    nir: { name: "NIR" }

parts.name: Atlas Scientific EZO-EC conductivity circuit + probe

i2c.how_to_change: Set by command. Deployed here at decimal 100 (0x64).

parts.calibration_notes: Dry calibration first, then two points bracketing your working range (typically 1413 uS/cm and 12.88 mS/cm). Set the probe's K value to match the physical probe or every reading is scaled wrong.
parts.evidence: Same single config as the EZO-pH, same history of abandoned attempts. Works; expensive; fiddly.
failure_modes: Wrong K value in the circuit silently scales every reading - it looks plausible and is wrong.
Salt build-up on the electrodes reads low over weeks.
Shares the ground-loop sensitivity of the whole EZO family in a pumped line.

parts.name: Atlas Scientific EZO-pH circuit + probe

i2c.how_to_change: Address is set by command over I2C or UART (any value 1-127). The deployed config uses decimal 99 (0x63) for pH, 102 (0x66) for RTD and 100 (0x64) for EC.

parts.protocol_settings: EZO circuits speak both I2C and UART; switch mode by shorting PGND to TX. I2C default 0x63 for pH.

price.note: Circuit plus lab-grade probe. The probe is the consumable and the expensive half.

parts.calibration_notes: Three-point (4.00 / 7.00 / 10.00) is the honest minimum for fertigation; two-point at 4 and 7 is acceptable if you never go alkaline. Recalibrate monthly. The probe is a consumable with a 12-24 month life in continuous nutrient service - a probe that will not calibrate is dead, not misbehaving.
parts.evidence: ONE device config, and an honest look at it tells the real story: atlas-reservoir.yaml contains three separate EZO configurations, two of them commented out, with only the third live. The facility spec confirms Atlas pH is reading in the irrigation room, so it does work - but three abandoned attempts in one file is a fair signal of how much effort it took. Single deployment plus that history keeps it out of field-proven.
failure_modes: Cost. A full pH/EC/RTD EZO stack is more than the entire rest of a monitoring node.
The probe is a consumable. Budget replacement annually in continuous service and do not be surprised by it.
Ground loops: a pumped nutrient line carries stray voltage that shifts pH readings. Atlas sell an isolator for exactly this and you will probably need it.
I2C address is software-set and stored on the circuit. Swap a circuit in and it arrives at whatever address the last person left it on.
Never let a pH probe dry out. Storage solution or it is scrap.
parts.notes: If you are starting fresh and only need trend data rather than compliance-grade numbers, an industrial RS485 pH transmitter is a fraction of the price. Choose EZO when you need the accuracy and the calibration audit trail.

example.title: EZO-pH on I2C with temperature compensation
example.code:
i2c:
  sda: GPIO23
  scl: GPIO22
  scan: true

sensor:
  - platform: ezo
    id: ph_probe
    address: 99            # decimal - EZO addresses are set by command, not straps
    unit_of_measurement: pH
    accuracy_decimals: 2
    update_interval: 10s
    name: Reservoir pH

  - platform: ezo
    id: rtd_probe
    address: 102
    unit_of_measurement: "\u00b0C"
    accuracy_decimals: 2
    update_interval: 10s
    name: Reservoir Temperature
    on_value:
      # pH is temperature dependent - push RTD temperature into the pH circuit
      - lambda: |-
          char buf[24];
          snprintf(buf, sizeof(buf), "T,%.2f", x);
          id(ph_probe).send_custom(buf);

# Disable the circuits' onboard LEDs on boot - they are bright and they age.
esphome:
  on_boot:
    priority: 700
    then:
      - lambda: |-
          id(ph_probe).send_custom("L,0");
          id(rtd_probe).send_custom("L,0");

parts.name: Atlas Scientific EZO-RTD temperature circuit + PT-1000 probe

i2c.how_to_change: Set by command. Deployed at decimal 102 (0x66).

parts.evidence: Deployed alongside the pH and EC circuits. Its real job is feeding temperature compensation into the other two - pH and EC are both strongly temperature dependent and uncompensated readings drift with the day.
failure_modes: Massive overkill if all you need is solution temperature - a DS18B20 does that for a twentieth of the price. Buy the RTD only because the EZO stack wants it.

parts.name: BH1750 ambient light sensor

i2c.how_to_change: ADDR pin low = 0x23, high = 0x5C. Two per bus, no more.

parts.calibration_notes: Reports lux, which is weighted to HUMAN photopic vision, not plant photosynthesis. Converting lux to PPFD needs a fixed multiplier per light spectrum, and that multiplier is different for HPS, white LED and blurple. It is a relative trend sensor unless you calibrate it against a real quantum sensor under your own fixtures.
parts.evidence: 2 configs run an active bh1750 block. Used here as a cheap 'are the lights actually on and at what relative level' check, not as a PPFD instrument - a commercial GrowSensor covers real PPFD/DLI in room 1.
failure_modes: Lux is not PPFD. Quoting a lux-derived PPFD number across different fixture spectra is meaningless.
Saturates around 65535 lx - directly under a modern LED bar it will peg and read flat.
Any dust or condensation on the window reads as a light-level drop, which looks exactly like a failing driver.
Only two addresses available, so three sensors on one bus needs a mux.
parts.notes: Excellent value for photoperiod verification and detecting a failed driver. For anything you intend to steer a crop on, buy a real quantum sensor - see cwt-ps-par or a commercial unit. Use this to answer 'did the lights come on', not 'what is my DLI'.

example.title: BH1750 as a photoperiod / driver-failure check
example.code:
i2c:
  id: bus_a
  sda: GPIO16
  scl: GPIO17

sensor:
  - platform: bh1750
    name: "Canopy light level"
    address: 0x23
    i2c_id: bus_a
    update_interval: 60s
    # Reported in lux. Do NOT publish a lux->PPFD conversion unless you have
    # calibrated the multiplier against a quantum sensor under YOUR fixtures.
    filters:
      - median:
          window_size: 5
          send_every: 5

parts.name: Bosch BME280 temperature / humidity / pressure sensor

i2c.how_to_change: SDO pin low = 0x76, high = 0x77. Most breakouts expose this as a solder jumper.

parts.evidence: Config blocks for it exist in the shared library (common/sensors/bme280.yaml and a 0x77 variant) but no current device includes them - the fleet standardised on SHT30 for humidity accuracy.
failure_modes: Humidity accuracy is +/-3% vs the SHT30's +/-2%. Small on paper, meaningful when it feeds a VPD setpoint.
Notorious for counterfeit BMP280 dies sold as BME280 - if humidity always reads 0, you bought a BMP280.
Self-heats noticeably if you poll it fast. Keep update_interval at 30s or slower.

parts.name: Bosch BME680 gas / T / RH / pressure sensor

i2c.how_to_change: SDO low = 0x76, high = 0x77.

parts.calibration_notes: The gas channel is a raw resistance, not a calibrated VOC concentration. It needs a burn-in of 24-48h and only ever means anything relative to its own recent history.
parts.evidence: One deployment in the drying room, where the gas-resistance trend is a cheap proxy for terpene off-gassing during cure. Treat it as a trend line, not a measurement.
failure_modes: The heater plate self-heats hard - its own temperature reading is useless as room temperature.
Gas resistance drifts with humidity as much as with VOC. Without compensation you are largely plotting RH.
Same 0x76/0x77 address space as the BME280 and BMP280 - three parts fighting over two addresses.

parts.name: Bosch BMP280 pressure & temperature sensor

i2c.how_to_change: SDO low = 0x76, high = 0x77.

parts.evidence: One deployment. Pressure only - no humidity. Useful for SCD4x ambient pressure compensation, which is worth a percent or two of CO2 accuracy at altitude.
failure_modes: No humidity channel. If you wanted humidity you wanted the BME280.

parts.name: Chill Division SDI-12 substrate sensor
parts.protocol_settings: SDI-12 probe with an integrated ESP node; auto-discovers over MQTT.

voltage.note: USB-powered node plus probe supply.

vendors.name: Chill Division (GitHub)
vendors.note: Open hardware/firmware - build it or buy it depending on availability.

parts.calibration_notes: The point of this one: it ships calibrated for soilless media, so you skip the regression exercise that every other probe in this category demands.
parts.evidence: Not deployed in this facility - the SDI-12 fleet was already built on bare probes before this existed. Carried over from the HAGR parts list as the recommendation for new builds precisely because it removes the calibration step that trips people up.
failure_modes: MQTT auto-discovery means you inherit whatever topic layout it chooses - fine with HA, more work if you are not using it.
Less transparent than a bare probe: if you disagree with its calibration you are editing firmware, not a lambda.

parts.name: CO2 cylinder regulator, flowmeter and mains solenoid set
parts.subcategory: CO2 injection regulator and electrically operated shutoff

voltage.note: The listed NZ set uses a 230 V solenoid with a local three-pin plug. The regulator and flowmeter are mechanical.

vendors.name: Growshop NZ CO2 regulator and solenoid set

parts.evidence: HAGR identifies this regulator and solenoid set as the unit in use. The current vendor listing confirms a 0-15 SCFH flowmeter, 0-4000 psi high-pressure gauge, 230 V solenoid, 4.2 mm hose tail and NZ hire-cylinder coupling. The regulator is not represented in ESPHome, so it is rated works rather than field-proven.
failure_modes: A solenoid stuck open can displace oxygen in an enclosed room. Use an independent CO2 alarm, occupancy and ventilation interlocks, and a short device-level dead-man timer. Home Assistant alone is not a life-safety controller.
Cylinder pressure does not report remaining liquid CO2 reliably; pressure stays nearly flat until the liquid is gone. Weigh the cylinder if remaining capacity matters.
Cylinder valve threads vary by country and gas supplier. Confirm the coupling matches the actual cylinder before ordering.
The listing gives no ingress rating for the solenoid. Keep the mains assembly dry and outside spray or condensation paths.
High sustained flow can chill or ice the regulator and change delivered flow. Size tubing and injection bursts rather than leaving the valve continuously energised.
parts.notes: The safe automation pattern is deliberately fail-closed. Restore outputs off after reboot, de-energise on network loss, cap every injection burst locally, and treat the room CO2 alarm as independent hardware. The flowmeter sets an approximate delivery rate; the SCD41 closes the control loop on measured room concentration.

parts.name: ComWinTop CWT-BL-EC-4400-S inline EC sensor
parts.protocol_settings: Modbus RTU, 4800 baud 8-N-1 factory default, slave address 1. EC plus a temperature register; temperature compensation is applied in-sensor on most firmware revisions.
parts.calibration_notes: Standard EC practice: 1413 uS/cm and 12.88 mS/cm standards, rinsed with distilled water between. The electrode fouls with nutrient salts - expect to reclean and recheck monthly in a fertigation line.
parts.evidence: Not deployed. Part of the ComWinTop rescue - family conventions confirmed, model register map not. The facility runs Atlas EZO and an Aqua Pro controller for EC instead.
failure_modes: Electrode fouling is the dominant failure. An unclean cell reads low and drifts slowly enough that you trust it.
Bubbles trapped across the electrodes give wild spikes - mount so flow sweeps them out, never in a dead leg.
If in-sensor temperature compensation is on and you ALSO compensate in software you will double-correct.
parts.notes:
ComWinTop (CWT) sell a whole family of cheap industrial RS485 Modbus sensors that are barely documented in English anywhere online - the manuals arrive as PDF email attachments and then vanish. This catalogue records the wiring and register maps so the next person does not have to reverse-engineer them.

Family conventions that hold across the range:
- Brown = V+ (typically 4.5-30V DC), Black = GND.
- RS485 A+/B- colours are NOT consistent between models. The LEAF-TH uses YELLOW for A+ and BLUE for B-, which is different from most of the others. Meter the pair before you trust the colour.
- Factory default is usually 4800 baud 8-N-1, slave address 1.
- Manuals list function code 0x30 in the register table but every worked example frame uses 0x03, so use `register_type: holding`. Fall back to `register_type: read` if you get timeouts.
- Calibration offsets live in the sensor's own holding registers and persist across power cycles - expose them as ESPHome `number` entities and you can trim a probe from Home Assistant without reflashing.

STATUS: register map unverified. PRs welcome.

parts.name: ComWinTop CWT-LEAF-TH-S-N leaf surface temperature & wetness sensor
parts.protocol_settings: Modbus RTU, 4800 baud 8-N-1, slave address 0x01 (factory defaults). Registers: 0x0000 wetness (0.1 %), 0x0001 leaf surface temperature (0.1 C, signed). Calibration offsets: 0x0050 temperature, 0x0051 wetness, both 0.1 units, read/write.

vendors.name: ComWinTop (Alibaba storefront)
vendors.note: Availability is erratic; quote by part number.

parts.calibration_notes: Two independent trims, both stored in the sensor. Temperature: settle it beside a trusted thermometer and enter the correction. Wetness: with the pad clean and bone dry it must read 0% - only trim if the dry baseline drifts. Do NOT try to make the wetness channel match an air hygrometer.
parts.evidence: One deployment on a PoESP32. Genuinely useful: leaf surface temperature is what leaf-VPD actually needs, and the wetness pad is a real disease-pressure signal. Single deployment keeps it out of field-proven.
failure_modes: The 'humidity' channel is leaf WETNESS - water sitting on a dielectric pad - not air humidity. The manual calls it %RH and that is misleading. A dry pad reads ~0%; it spikes on dew and misting.
Wiring colour trap: this model uses YELLOW for RS485 A+, unlike most of the CWT range. Miswire it and you get silence.
Manual documents function code 0x30 which does not exist; the real frames use 0x03. Use register_type: holding.
Negative temperatures are sent as two's complement - read as S_WORD or sub-zero readings wrap to ~6553C.
The pad reads the pad, not a leaf. Placement matters more than calibration - clipped in canopy, shaded, same aspect as the leaves you care about.

example.title: CWT-LEAF-TH over RS485, with in-sensor calibration exposed to HA
example.code:
# Wiring: Brown = V+ (4.5-30V) | Black = GND | YELLOW = A+ | BLUE = B-
# (yellow-for-A+ is specific to this model - meter it, do not assume)
# RS485 via the PoESP32 Grove port: GPIO17 = TXD, GPIO16 = RXD

uart:
  id: uart_bus
  tx_pin: 17
  rx_pin: 16
  baud_rate: 4800        # factory default per manual
  stop_bits: 1

modbus:
  uart_id: uart_bus
  id: modbus_hub

modbus_controller:
  - id: leaf_probe
    address: 0x01        # factory default slave address
    modbus_id: modbus_hub
    setup_priority: -10
    update_interval: 10s

sensor:
  # 0x0000 - leaf WETNESS (water on the pad), 0.1 % per count.
  # The manual calls this %RH. It is not air humidity.
  - platform: modbus_controller
    modbus_controller_id: leaf_probe
    name: Leaf Wetness
    address: 0x0000
    register_type: holding    # manual says 0x30; real frames use 0x03
    value_type: U_WORD
    unit_of_measurement: "%"
    state_class: measurement
    accuracy_decimals: 1
    filters:
      - multiply: 0.1

  # 0x0001 - leaf surface temperature, 0.1 C per count, SIGNED.
  - platform: modbus_controller
    modbus_controller_id: leaf_probe
    name: Leaf Surface Temperature
    address: 0x0001
    register_type: holding
    value_type: S_WORD        # S_WORD or sub-zero readings wrap
    unit_of_measurement: "\u00b0C"
    device_class: temperature
    state_class: measurement
    accuracy_decimals: 1
    filters:
      - multiply: 0.1

number:
  # Offsets live in the sensor's own registers and survive power cycles.
  # lambda scales the raw register for display; multiply scales it back on write.
  - platform: modbus_controller
    modbus_controller_id: leaf_probe
    name: Leaf Temp Calibration Offset
    register_type: holding
    address: 0x0050
    value_type: S_WORD
    unit_of_measurement: "\u00b0C"
    entity_category: config
    min_value: -10
    max_value: 10
    step: 0.1
    lambda: "return x * 0.1;"
    multiply: 10

  - platform: modbus_controller
    modbus_controller_id: leaf_probe
    name: Leaf Wetness Calibration Offset
    register_type: holding
    address: 0x0051
    value_type: S_WORD
    unit_of_measurement: "%"
    entity_category: config
    min_value: -20
    max_value: 20
    step: 0.1
    lambda: "return x * 0.1;"
    multiply: 10

parts.name: DFRobot Gravity analog ORP sensor

voltage.note: Analog output referenced to the supply rail - a noisy 5V rail becomes a noisy ORP reading.

parts.calibration_notes: Single-point against a 220mV or 470mV ORP standard. The offset drifts, so recheck monthly if the number is doing anything more than trending.
parts.evidence: One pilot node. ORP is genuinely useful for tracking hypochlorous/peroxide sanitiser residual in a recirculating system, but this is an analog probe on an ESP32 ADC - the noise floor limits what you can honestly claim from it.
failure_modes: ESP32 ADC is nonlinear and noisy. Without averaging and a decent reference the last 20mV are fiction.
The platinum electrode passivates with organic film - it reads increasingly sluggish rather than obviously wrong.
Shares the pumped-line ground-loop problem; an isolated supply helps a lot.
ORP in a nutrient tank is dominated by whatever sanitiser you dosed last, not by anything about the plants.

parts.name: DS18B20 1-Wire temperature probe
parts.protocol_settings: 1-Wire, each device has a unique 64-bit ROM address. 4.7k pull-up to 3V3 on the data line.

voltage.note: Use normal power, not parasite power - parasite mode is a common source of flaky reads.

price.note: Waterproof stainless probe on a 1-3 m lead.

parts.calibration_notes: Factory accuracy +/-0.5 C over -10 to +85 C. Good enough for tank and root-zone water without user calibration.
parts.evidence: No active dallas/one_wire block in the current fleet - reservoir temperature is read off the Atlas RTD and the substrate probes instead. Included because it is the cheapest reliable way to get water temperature and it is what most growers will reach for first.
failure_modes: Counterfeit DS18B20s are everywhere and are genuinely bad - wrong resolution, +/-2 C errors, and they drop off the bus intermittently. Buy from a real distributor.
Parasite power looks like it works then fails under load; run a proper 3-wire connection.
Long leads without the 4.7k pull-up (or with it at the wrong end) give intermittent CRC errors that look like a dying probe.
The stainless sheath is earthed in some probes - dropping one into a tank with a stray-voltage problem can inject noise into your EC reading.
parts.notes: Rock solid when genuine and wired properly. Many probes can share one GPIO since each has a unique ROM address, which makes it cheap to instrument several tanks at once. In ESPHome 2025.x+ the component is `one_wire` + `dallas_temp`, not the old `dallas`.

example.title: DS18B20 water temperature (modern one_wire component)
example.code:
# NOTE: the old `platform: dallas` was removed in ESPHome 2025.x.
# Use the one_wire bus + dallas_temp sensor instead.
one_wire:
  - platform: gpio
    pin: GPIO32          # needs a 4.7k pull-up to 3V3

sensor:
  - platform: dallas_temp
    # Find the address in the logs on first boot, then pin it here so a
    # second probe on the bus cannot silently swap identities.
    address: 0x0000000000000000
    name: "Reservoir temperature"
    resolution: 12
    update_interval: 30s

parts.name: Float switch (tank level interlock)

voltage.note: Dry contact - wire to a GPIO with INPUT_PULLUP and let the float pull it to ground.

price.note: Receipt price for a small vertical float switch. A heavier-duty variant on the same receipt was NZ$66.43 - if you need a long stem or a higher switching current, budget for that end instead.

parts.evidence: One deployment as a runoff-tank high-level interlock. Dumb, cheap, and the thing you actually want guarding a pump - an ultrasonic sensor tells you a story, a float switch tells you the truth.
failure_modes: Sticks when gunged up with root debris or biofilm. Test it periodically rather than assuming.
Contact bounce - debounce with delayed_on/delayed_off filters or you will get phantom trips.
A single float gives one threshold. Two floats (low and high) is usually what you actually need.
parts.notes: Best practice: use the ultrasonic sensor for the number and the float switch for the interlock. Never let a computed level be the only thing standing between a pump and a dry run.

example.title: Debounced float switch as a pump interlock
example.code:
binary_sensor:
  - platform: gpio
    pin:
      number: GPIO32
      mode: INPUT_PULLUP
      inverted: true
    name: Tank Float
    id: tank_level
    filters:
      - delayed_on: 50ms      # contact bounce is real
      - delayed_off: 50ms
    on_press:
      - switch.turn_off: transfer_pump   # hard interlock, on-device

parts.name: Metric food-grade push-to-connect check valve (10 mm)
parts.protocol_settings: 10 mm push-to-connect. Directional - flow arrow must point away from the stock tank.
parts.evidence: On the dosing lines out of the peristaltic heads. Cheap protection against the failure where a stock concentrate siphons back into a shared line.
failure_modes: Fitted backwards it silently blocks the dose - the pump runs, reports success, and nothing arrives.
Cracking pressure is not zero; a very low-flow peristaltic head may struggle to open it, so check the head can actually shift it.
Non-food-grade equivalents leach into nutrient concentrate and perish in acid.
parts.notes: The reason to fit one is not the pump - it is the shared manifold. Without a check valve per dosing line, concentrated pH-down can migrate up another pump's line into a different stock container, which ruins the stock and is genuinely hazardous to handle.

parts.name: Growlink TerraLink substrate probe
parts.protocol_settings: SDI-12, 1200 baud 7-E-1 inverted half-duplex. Deployed at sensor address 1.

vendors.name: Growlink
vendors.note: Sold as part of their controller ecosystem; standalone availability varies by region.

parts.calibration_notes: Reads about 24% high against a TEROS 12 in the same block on the same substrate. The deployed config applies a provisional one-point scale of 0.806 to align it to TEROS. Do your own regression against a reference probe before trusting the absolute number - the SHAPE of the dryback is right, the absolute value is not.
parts.evidence: Three deployed probes. Works reliably on the same SDI-12 stack as everything else, but only after being regressed against a TEROS 12 - the raw numbers are not interchangeable.
failure_modes: Reads high vs TEROS 12 on identical substrate. If you mix probe brands across rooms and compare setpoints, you will make bad irrigation decisions.
Same Hilhorst dry-media blow-up as any dielectric probe.
Vendor documentation for the raw SDI-12 interface is thin - most of what is known here came from probing the bus.
parts.notes: The deployed config carries BOTH a raw VWC and an aligned VWC channel, so the correction is visible and auditable rather than baked silently into one number. Worth copying that habit.

example.title: TerraLink with the TEROS-alignment channel kept visible

parts.name: Hunter PGV 24 VAC irrigation solenoid valve
parts.protocol_settings: 24 VAC coil, ~0.3 A inrush / ~0.2 A hold. Switch with a relay or triac, never a DC output.

voltage.note: 24 VAC ONLY. A 24 VDC supply will buzz the coil and eventually cook it.

parts.evidence: The zone valve behind the relay nodes in this fleet - six configs drive 24 VAC valves through relay boards. Bought repeatedly at the same trade price across separate purchase lines, which is a fair sign it is the settled choice rather than a trial.
failure_modes: Grit under the diaphragm holds the valve part-open and it weeps continuously - fit a screen filter upstream, which is cheaper than the callout.
The solenoid can be unscrewed under pressure by accident during manual bleeding, which dumps the line.
24 VAC coils hum audibly; in a quiet room that reads as a fault when it is normal.
Fails OPEN if the diaphragm perforates - the software safety pattern cannot save you here, so put a master valve or a normally-closed contactor upstream.
parts.notes: Pair with a 24 VAC transformer sized for simultaneous zones (see transformer-24vac). Inrush is roughly 3x hold current, so a transformer that runs three valves steady-state may still brown out when they all pull in together - stagger the switch-on. Everything driving one of these must carry the flood-safety pattern in SAFETY.md.

parts.name: HX711 24-bit load cell amplifier

voltage.note: Runs happily at 3.3V but resolution improves at 5V. Its two-wire interface is bit-banged, not real I2C or SPI.

parts.calibration_notes: Tare empty, then apply a known mass and record the scale factor. Both values belong in persistent globals so a reboot does not lose the calibration.
parts.evidence: Four deployments weighing CO2 cylinders. Cylinder mass is the only honest way to know how much CO2 you have left - regulator pressure tells you almost nothing until the liquid is gone.
failure_modes: Temperature drift. The HX711 and the load cell both drift; a cylinder that 'loses' 200g overnight in a room that cooled 8C has not leaked.
The bit-banged interface is timing sensitive. WiFi interrupts on a busy ESP cause dropped reads - the 10SPS rate is more stable than 80SPS.
Cheap load cells creep under sustained load. A cylinder sat on one for months reads progressively low.
Mechanical mounting dominates accuracy. A cell that is loaded off-axis or bridging on its cable is unfixable in software.

example.title: HX711 CO2 cylinder scale
example.code:
sensor:
  - platform: hx711
    name: CO2 Cylinder Mass
    dout_pin: GPIO13
    clk_pin: GPIO14
    gain: 128
    update_interval: 5s
    unit_of_measurement: kg
    accuracy_decimals: 2
    filters:
      # scale factor from your two-point calibration
      - calibrate_linear:
          - 0 -> 0.0
          - 438500 -> 25.0
      # load cells are noisy - a median over a window beats a single read
      - median:
          window_size: 9
          send_every: 3

parts.name: Infiwin MT22 SDI-12 substrate probe
parts.protocol_settings: SDI-12, 1200 baud 7-E-1 inverted half-duplex. Deployed at sensor address 0. Returns a RAW count on index 1 (not VWC), temperature on 2, bulk EC in uS/cm on 3.

price.note: Roughly a fifth of a TEROS 12. That price gap is the entire reason to bother calibrating it.

vendors.name: AliExpress (search Infiwin MT22 SDI-12)
vendors.note: Listing rot is severe here. Search the part number, not a saved link.

parts.calibration_notes: Index 1 is a raw dielectric count, NOT a percentage - publishing it as VWC is the classic mistake. The deployed cubic converting raw counts to volumetric water content in coco is in the example. Bulk EC comes back in uS/cm, so divide by 1000 before feeding anything that expects dS/m.
parts.evidence: Six probes carrying the whole of room 1's crop-steering substrate data - two per row across three rows. The cheap probe that actually earned its place, once calibrated.
failure_modes: Raw counts on index 1 look plausible as a percentage and are not. Publish that unconverted and your dryback targets are meaningless.
EC units differ from the TEROS family (uS/cm vs dS/m) - a 1000x error waiting to happen in a shared dashboard.
Build quality is what you pay for: cable entry is the failure point. Keep the gland out of standing water.
No published calibration from the vendor. Every number below is somebody's regression, including this one.

example.title: MT22 raw-count to VWC, plus the uS/cm to dS/m fix
example.code:
sensor:
  - platform: sdi12
    address: 0
    update_interval: 30s
    sensors:
      - index: 1
        name: RAW VWC
        id: mt22_raw
        accuracy_decimals: 0
        internal: true        # raw counts - never publish this as a percentage
      - index: 2
        name: Substrate Temperature
        id: mt22_temp
        unit_of_measurement: "\u00b0C"
        device_class: temperature
        state_class: measurement
        accuracy_decimals: 1
      - index: 3
        name: Bulk EC
        id: mt22_bulk_ec_uS
        unit_of_measurement: "\u00b5S/cm"
        state_class: measurement
        accuracy_decimals: 0

  - platform: template
    name: VWC
    id: mt22_vwc
    unit_of_measurement: "%"
    accuracy_decimals: 2
    state_class: measurement
    update_interval: 30s
    lambda: |-
      float R = id(mt22_raw).state;
      if (isnan(R) || R <= 0) return NAN;
      float theta = 6.771e-10f*R*R*R - 5.105e-6f*R*R + 1.302e-2f*R - 10.848f;
      float pct = theta * 100.0f;
      if (pct < 0) pct = 0;
      if (pct > 100) pct = 100;
      return pct;

  # Normalise to dS/m so it can be compared with TEROS-family probes.
  - platform: template
    name: Bulk EC (dS/m)
    unit_of_measurement: dS/m
    accuracy_decimals: 2
    update_interval: 30s
    lambda: |-
      float e = id(mt22_bulk_ec_uS).state;
      if (isnan(e)) return NAN;
      return e / 1000.0f;

parts.name: KinCony F16 16-channel relay controller

i2c.how_to_change: On-board PCF8574 expanders; address set by solder jumpers.

parts.protocol_settings: RS485 Modbus RTU, slave address discovered by scan. W5500 SPI Ethernet.

voltage.note: DIN-rail unit, relay contacts rated 10A.

parts.evidence: HALL OF SHAME (with an asterisk). Exactly one config, and that config STILL CONTAINS a brute-force Modbus address scanner - it walks slave addresses looking for the board because the address was never pinned down. A config that is still probing for its own device is not a config you should copy.
failure_modes: The live config carries a leftover brute-force address scanner - the Modbus slave address was never determined and committed.
Sixteen channels on one node is a large blast radius: one failed board takes out sixteen loads at once.
Documentation is thin and largely machine-translated; pinouts differ between hardware revisions sold under the same name.
Its W5500 Ethernet needs a different ESPHome config from the IP101 PHY used everywhere else in this fleet - an easy way to lose an afternoon.
parts.notes: Attractive on price-per-channel and it is genuinely DIN-rail mountable, which the M5Stack units are not. But concentrate irrigation on one 16-channel board and a single failure floods everything. This fleet deliberately uses several 4-channel nodes instead. If you do deploy it, pin the Modbus address and delete the scanner.

example.title: What NOT to ship - the address scanner still in the live config
example.code:
# ANTI-PATTERN - do not copy this into production.
# This is a brute-force Modbus slave-address scanner that is still present in
# the one live F16 config. It exists because the board's address was never
# pinned down. Symptoms of shipping it: bus noise, slow startup, and a device
# whose identity changes if anything else joins the RS485 segment.
#
#   interval:
#     - interval: 2s
#       then:
#         - lambda: |-
#             static uint8_t addr = 1;
#             ESP_LOGW("scan", "trying modbus address %d", addr);
#             addr++;                       # walks 1..247 forever
#
# Do this instead: find the address ONCE with a Modbus scanning tool, then
# hard-code it and delete the scanner.
modbus_controller:
  - id: f16
    address: 0x01        # pinned, not discovered
    modbus_id: modbus_hub
    update_interval: 5s

parts.name: Load cell (50kg half-bridge or 200kg bar)

voltage.note: Excited by the HX711 - no separate supply.

parts.evidence: Paired with the HX711 on all four scale nodes. Size the cell to the load: a full 25kg CO2 cylinder on a 200kg bar wastes most of your resolution.
failure_modes: Overload past the rated capacity permanently deforms the gauge. There is no recovery and no error - it just reads wrong forever.
Half-bridge 50kg cells (the flat bathroom-scale type) need to be used in fours, or with a matching dummy resistor pair. Used singly they are wildly nonlinear.
Moisture ingress at the cable entry drifts the bridge. In a wet room, seal it.

parts.name: M5Stack ENV III Unit (SHT30 + QMP6988)

i2c.how_to_change:
Two chips, two addresses. The SHT30 half moves 0x44 -> 0x45 by pulling ADDR high. The QMP6988
half sits at 0x70 and can move to 0x56. 0x70 is also the TCA9548A default, so adding a
multiplexer later collides with this module unless you move one of them first.

parts.evidence: The standard climate pairing here: an SCD41 for CO2 plus an ENV III for the temperature and humidity that actually drive VPD, because the SCD41's own T/RH self-heats. Four deployments.
failure_modes: QMP6988 defaults to 0x70, the same address as the TCA9548A mux. Add a mux to an existing ENV III node and the bus goes strange - move one of them.
The Grove cable is the weak point: >1m runs at 100kHz get flaky. Drop to 50kHz.
Not condensing-rated. In a drying room at high RH the SHT30 will read 100% and stay there until it dries out.
use_cases: room T/RH/pressure in one Grove unit

example.title: ENV III - SHT30 + QMP6988 on one Grove port
example.code:
sensor:
  - platform: sht3xd
    address: 0x44
    update_interval: 30s
    heater_enabled: false
    temperature:
      name: Room Temperature
      filters:
        - lambda: |-
            if (-40.0 <= x && x <= 100.0) return x;
            else return {};
    humidity:
      name: Room Humidity
      filters:
        - lambda: |-
            if (0.0 <= x && x <= 100.0) return x;
            else return {};

  - platform: qmp6988
    address: 0x70          # NOTE: same default as a TCA9548A mux - move one if you use both
    update_interval: 30s
    temperature:
      name: ENV III Temperature
      internal: true
    pressure:
      name: Barometric Pressure

parts.name: M5Stack 2-channel SPST relay unit

i2c.how_to_change: Solder jumpers select the address. Note 0x26 is the 4-Relay default, so check the collision map before pairing the two on one bus.

voltage.note: Contacts rated 250 VAC / 10 A nominal - derate hard for inductive loads.

parts.evidence: Not currently deployed - this fleet standardised on the 4-channel unit. Catalogued because two channels is often the honest requirement, and a smaller module means a smaller blast radius when it fails.
failure_modes: Same welded-contact risk as any relay driving an inductive load - fit a snubber or drive a contactor.
Default 0x25 is one address away from the 4-Relay's 0x26; mixing them without checking is an easy collision.
Restores its previous state on boot unless told otherwise - force restore_mode ALWAYS_OFF on anything that moves water or gas.
parts.notes: Everything in SAFETY.md applies here exactly as it does to the 4-channel unit. Fewer channels is a feature for anything critical: one failed module takes out two loads rather than four.

parts.name: M5Stack 4-Relay Unit

i2c.how_to_change: Solder jumpers on the back select 0x26-0x2F, so up to 10 modules (40 relays) can share one bus.

voltage.note: Contacts rated 250VAC/10A or 30VDC/10A, but derate hard for inductive loads.

price.note: Trade price from a purchase receipt. The M5Stack list price for the same unit is around NZ$33, so this reflects a distributor rate rather than RRP.

parts.evidence: 18 production configs drive an active m5stack4relay block - irrigation solenoids, ceiling vents, dehumidifiers, CO2 and dry-room relays. This is the workhorse output device of the facility and it is the part most tightly bound to the SAFETY pattern.
failure_modes: Relay channel numbering is REVERSED relative to the silkscreen in the ESPHome external component - relay4 is physical relay 1. Get this wrong and you open the wrong valve.
Default restore_mode restores the last state on boot; after a power cut that can silently re-open an irrigation valve. Always force ALWAYS_OFF.
Contacts weld closed under repeated inductive switching (solenoids, contactors) - fit a snubber or drive a proper contactor instead of the load directly.
Needs an external component - it is not in ESPHome core.
parts.notes: Anything on this module that can move water or gas MUST carry the three-part safety pattern: restore_mode ALWAYS_OFF, an on_turn_on auto-shutoff delay, and a network killguard. See SAFETY.md - that pattern is the single highest-value thing in this repo.

example.title: 4-Relay with the full flood-safety pattern
example.source: distilled from room-1-irrigation-relays.yaml (channel order verified against that config)
example.code:
external_components:
  - source:
      type: git
      url: https://github.com/KoenBreeman/ESPHome_custom_components/
      ref: main
    components: [m5stack4relay]

i2c:
  id: main_i2c
  sda: GPIO16
  scl: GPIO17
  scan: true

# Flood safety: kill outputs only on a SUSTAINED network loss, so brief
# Ethernet flaps do not interrupt a live feed. mode: restart re-arms the window.
script:
  - id: disconnect_killguard
    mode: restart
    then:
      - delay: 90s
      - logger.log: "Sustained network loss >90s - flood safety: all valves off"
      - switch.turn_off: relay_1

switch:
  - platform: m5stack4relay
    sync_mode: true
    id: four_relays
    i2c_id: main_i2c
    # NOTE: relay4: here is PHYSICAL relay 1. The mapping is reversed.
    relay4:
      id: relay_1
      name: "Zone 1 valve"
      restore_mode: ALWAYS_OFF        # never resume a valve after a power cut
      on_turn_on:                     # dead-man timer: max feed length
        - delay: 1200s
        - switch.turn_off: relay_1

parts.name: M5Stack AirQ (SEN55 + SCD40 air quality node)

i2c.how_to_change:
Fixed. The AirQ carries three chips on one internal bus: SEN55 at 0x69, SCD4x at 0x62 and a
PCF8563 RTC at 0x51. None are strappable, so two AirQ boards cannot share one external bus,
and it collides with any discrete SEN55, SCD4x or PCF8563 you add alongside it.

voltage.note: USB-C or internal LiPo.

parts.calibration_notes: SCD4x wants forced recalibration in fresh air roughly annually; SEN55 VOC/NOx run a self-learning baseline that needs ~12h of representative air before its index means anything.
parts.evidence: Seven of these are permanently installed one per room (two flower rooms, a veg room, a dry room and three back-of-house spaces) and have run continuously as the facility's ambient-air reference. Eight configs total.
failure_modes: The SEN55 fan pulls room air across the element - in a grow room it loads up with trichome and dust and PM readings drift high. Budget an annual clean.
Reported temperature runs warm because the board self-heats. Every deployment marks it internal: true and takes temperature from a separate SCD41 or SHT30.
Three fixed I2C addresses on one board (0x69, 0x62, 0x51) means two AirQ units cannot share an external bus without a mux.
VOC and NOx are unitless indices, not concentrations. They are only meaningful relative to their own learned baseline.
use_cases: CO2 plus particulate in one node

parts.name: M5Stack ATOM Lite (ESP32-PICO)

voltage.note: USB-C powered, 3.3V logic on the Grove and header pins.

parts.evidence: Carries the entire SDI-12 substrate fleet - one ATOM per probe, 14 units. Cheap enough to put one at every probe rather than run long analogue cable back to a central board.
failure_modes: WiFi-only. Fine for a sensor that can miss a reading; never put an irrigation valve on one.
The single onboard button is GPIO39 and is input-only - no internal pullup on some revisions.
USB-C power means a wall wart per probe. In a wet room that is a lot of GFCI-adjacent plugs; PoE is tidier at scale.
Onboard RGB LED shares GPIO27; driving it from esp32_rmt_led_strip while doing tight UART timing can jitter SDI-12 reads.
parts.notes: For SDI-12 the ATOM is wired single-pin half-duplex on GPIO26 - see the meter-teros12 and infiwin-mt22 entries for the exact UART block.

parts.name: M5Stack Atom PWM DC driver
parts.subcategory: Single-channel MOSFET PWM base with Atom Lite controller

voltage.note: The base accepts 12-24 V DC and M5Stack rates its switched output to 100 W maximum. GPIO22 drives the onboard PWM stage.

parts.evidence: One HAGR ESPHome config drives the Atom PWM on GPIO22 at 1 kHz and exposes it as a monochromatic Home Assistant light. M5Stack documentation identifies the current product as Atom PWM K065 and confirms the GPIO22 pin map, 12-24 V input and 100 W MOSFET output.
failure_modes: This is a low-side DC MOSFET driver, not an isolated 0-10 V lighting interface. Do not connect it to an unknown dimming pair until the driver manual confirms PWM or contact-closure compatibility and a safe common reference.
The 100 W rating is for a DC load under suitable thermal conditions. It is not permission to switch a grow light's mains input or full LED-driver output.
A shared ground can import noise or fault voltage from a lighting driver into the ESP32. Use an opto-isolated interface when the driver's dimming input is not explicitly SELV and common-ground safe.
PWM polarity differs between drivers. An inverted output can make 0 percent command full brightness; verify the off state before connecting the crop light.
WiFi loss must not leave a light at an unsafe state. Pair the dimming channel with a hard photoperiod cutoff or contactor that does not depend on this node.
parts.notes: Use this only on the low-voltage control side of a compatible driver. The HAGR example uses ESPHome LEDC at 1 kHz with inverted output. Confirm frequency, polarity and electrical interface against the exact lighting-driver datasheet before copying it.

example.title: Atom PWM exposed as a Home Assistant light
example.code:
output:
  - platform: ledc
    pin: GPIO22
    frequency: 1000 Hz
    id: grow_light_pwm
    inverted: true  # verify this against the exact driver before use

light:
  - platform: monochromatic
    name: "Grow light PWM"
    output: grow_light_pwm
    gamma_correct: 1.0

parts.name: M5Stack AtomS3 Lite (ESP32-S3)
parts.evidence: Widely used for newer nodes. Native USB makes flashing painless and the S3 has the RAM headroom the ESP32 classic runs out of on thermal-camera and voice work.
failure_modes: Native USB CDC means the serial port disappears on reboot - set a longer upload timeout or use OTA.
S3 pin numbering differs from the classic ATOM. Copy-pasting an ATOM Lite config will silently target the wrong pins.

parts.name: M5Stack Dial (round display + rotary encoder + RFID)

i2c.how_to_change:
Fixed internal bus on GPIO11/GPIO12: RC522 NFC at 0x28, FT5x06 touch controller at 0x38 and an
RTC at 0x51. Adding a discrete RC522 to the same bus collides at 0x28.

parts.evidence: Used as the at-the-tank readout: CO2 cylinder scales, batch tank level and a bench SDI-12 probe tester. Being able to read a number without opening a laptop is worth more in a wet room than it sounds.
failure_modes: Its internal I2C is GPIO11/GPIO12 and already carries three devices. Hanging external sensors off the same bus causes address clashes with anything at 0x28, 0x38 or 0x51.
The screen is the power hog - on battery it is hours, not days. Treat it as a mains device.
Rotary encoder detents are read in software; a busy display refresh can drop steps.

parts.name: M5Stack PoESP32 / ESP32 Ethernet unit (IP101G PHY)
parts.subcategory: PoE ESP32 node with wired Ethernet PHY

voltage.note: 802.3af PoE in, regulated 5V/3V3 out to the ESP32. Also runnable off plain 5V.

parts.evidence: 48 of 149 production configs declare `ethernet: type: IP101` with the M5Stack pin map (mdc GPIO23, mdio GPIO18, clk GPIO0_IN, power GPIO5). Every load-bearing actuator in the facility - irrigation valves, CO2, dehumidifiers, lighting contactors - runs wired rather than WiFi, and that is a deliberate reliability decision.
failure_modes: Short Ethernet flaps are common on cheap unmanaged switches; if you kill outputs instantly on on_disconnect you WILL interrupt live feeds. Use a grace timer - see the SAFETY.md killguard pattern.
power_pin GPIO5 must be driven or the PHY never comes up - symptom is a device that boots and reboots with no link.
PoE injectors that are not 802.3af-compliant (passive 24V) will not power it and can damage the unit.
GPIO0 is the PHY clock input, so it is unavailable for anything else and affects boot strapping.
parts.notes: This is the backbone of the facility. Wired Ethernet removes the entire class of 'WiFi dropped and the valve stayed open' failures. The IP101G pin map below is identical in all 48 configs - copy it verbatim. Note the newer M5Stack PoE modules ship a W5500 SPI MAC instead of the IP101 RMII PHY; the ESPHome config is different (see w5500-ethernet).

example.title: IP101 Ethernet - the exact pin map used on all 48 nodes
example.code:
ethernet:
  type: IP101
  mdc_pin: GPIO23
  mdio_pin: GPIO18
  clk_mode: GPIO0_IN
  phy_addr: 1
  power_pin: GPIO5
  # Do NOT de-energise outputs directly here - brief flaps are normal.
  # Start a grace timer instead, and cancel it if the link comes back.
  on_connect:
    - script.stop: disconnect_killguard
  on_disconnect:
    - script.execute: disconnect_killguard

text_sensor:
  - platform: ethernet_info
    ip_address:
      name: IP
    mac_address:
      name: MAC

parts.name: METER TEROS 12 substrate VWC / EC / temperature probe
parts.protocol_settings: SDI-12 v1.4. 1200 baud, 7-E-1, inverted, half-duplex on a single data wire. Default sensor address 0. Returns raw counts, bulk EC (dS/m) and temperature (C).

voltage.note: Runs from 4-15V. A 3.3V ESP32 rail technically works but readings get noisy - give it a proper supply.

price.note: The reference-grade option. This is why the cheaper SDI-12 clones exist.

parts.calibration_notes: Factory calibration is for mineral soil (Topp). In coco or rockwool the Topp equation UNDERESTIMATES badly - you need a soilless calibration. The deployed cubic for soilless media is in the example below. For pore-water EC use the Hilhorst model with eps0 = 4.1, and treat the result as invalid below 10% VWC (METER's own guidance) rather than publishing a garbage number.
parts.evidence: SDI-12 substrate sensing is the single largest sensor deployment after CO2: 14 nodes, one per probe. TEROS 12 is the reference the cheaper probes in this catalogue are regressed against.
failure_modes: Topp calibration in coco/rockwool reads low by 20%+ - you will steer generative when you are actually wet.
Pore-water EC via Hilhorst blows up as VWC approaches zero (the eb - eps0 denominator goes to zero). Clamp the denominator and return NaN below 10% VWC.
Needles must be fully in contact with substrate. An air gap from a badly seated probe reads permanently dry and no amount of recalibration fixes it.
Half-duplex single-wire UART is fussy: get the inversion or the 7-E-1 framing wrong and you get silence, not an error.
One probe per ESP is the pattern here. Multi-drop SDI-12 works in theory but address collisions on a shared wire are miserable to debug in a live room.
parts.notes: Bus-level gotcha that costs people days: ESPHome's built-in UART cannot do half-duplex on one pin. You need ssieb's `uarthalf` fork AND the `sdi12` component. Both are pinned in the example.

accuracy.conditions: Generic calibration - typical in mineral soils that have solution EC.
Medium-specific calibration, in any porous medium. This is why the repo keeps telling you to calibrate against your own substrate.

example.title: SDI-12 probe with soilless VWC and Hilhorst pore-water EC
example.code:
# SDI-12 is 1200 baud, 7 data bits, EVEN parity, 1 stop bit, INVERTED,
# half-duplex on a SINGLE wire. ESPHome core UART cannot do half-duplex,
# so both of these external components are required.
external_components:
  - source: github://ssieb/esphome@uarthalf
    components: [uart]
    refresh: 1min
  - source: github://ssieb/esphome_components@sdi12
    components: [sdi12]
    refresh: 1min

uart:
  - id: sdi12uart
    tx_pin:
      number: GPIO26      # single data wire - tx and rx are the same pin
      inverted: true
    baud_rate: 1200
    data_bits: 7
    parity: even
    stop_bits: 1
    half_duplex: true

sdi12:
  - id: sdibus
    uart_id: sdi12uart

sensor:
  - platform: sdi12
    address: 1                 # probe's SDI-12 address
    update_interval: 30s
    sensors:
      - index: 1
        name: Apparent Permittivity
        id: eps_b
        accuracy_decimals: 2
      - index: 2
        name: Bulk EC
        id: bulk_ec
        unit_of_measurement: dS/m
        accuracy_decimals: 2
      - index: 3
        name: Substrate Temperature
        id: sub_temp
        unit_of_measurement: "\u00b0C"
        accuracy_decimals: 1

  # Soilless (coco/rockwool) cubic. The factory Topp equation is for mineral
  # soil and reads badly low in soilless media.
  - platform: template
    name: Substrate VWC
    id: vwc
    unit_of_measurement: "%"
    accuracy_decimals: 2
    update_interval: 30s
    lambda: |-
      float e = id(eps_b).state;
      if (isnan(e) || e <= 0) return NAN;
      float theta = (5.5728e-6f*e*e*e) + (-6.40228e-4f*e*e)
                  + (2.98804e-2f*e) + 2.14996e-2f;
      float pct = theta * 100.0f;
      if (pct < 0) pct = 0;
      if (pct > 100) pct = 100;
      return pct;

  # Hilhorst pore-water EC, with METER's recommended eps0 and their validity guard.
  - platform: template
    name: Pore Water EC
    unit_of_measurement: dS/m
    accuracy_decimals: 2
    update_interval: 30s
    lambda: |-
      float sb  = id(bulk_ec).state;
      float T   = id(sub_temp).state;
      float eb  = id(eps_b).state;
      float wpc = id(vwc).state;
      if (isnan(sb) || isnan(T) || isnan(eb) || isnan(wpc)) return NAN;
      if (wpc < 10.0f) return NAN;        // METER: unreliable below 0.10 VWC

      float sb_25 = sb / (1.0f + 0.019f * (T - 25.0f));   // normalise to 25C
      float ep    = 80.3f - 0.37f * (T - 20.0f);          // pore water dielectric
      const float eps0 = 4.1f;
      float denom = eb - eps0;
      if (denom < 0.5f) denom = 0.5f;     // stop the blow-up in dry media
      return (ep * sb_25) / denom;

parts.name: MFRC522 / RC522 13.56 MHz RFID reader

i2c.how_to_change: I2C address is strapped by the EA/ADR pins on the module. Many cheap breakouts hard-wire SPI only and cannot do I2C at all - check before buying.

voltage.note: 3V3 ONLY. 5V on the RC522 kills it. Level-shift if your MCU is 5V.

price.note: Clone modules are a few dollars; quality varies wildly.

vendors.name: M5Stack RFID2 Unit (WS1850S)
vendors.note: I2C Grove version, more consistent than bare clones

vendors.name: AliExpress RC522 modules
vendors.note: Listing rot is guaranteed - search the part number, not the link

parts.evidence: 19 production configs reference RFID, 13 of them with an active rc522 platform block. Door access across two flower rooms, a veg room, a dry room and two back-of-house doors all run on this reader over PoE nodes, logging tag scans into Home Assistant.
failure_modes: 5V on VCC destroys the module instantly - it is 3V3 only and the silkscreen often does not say so.
Read range is 2-4 cm at best; a thick door plate or a metal backing plate drops it to nothing.
Cheap clones have poor antenna tuning and intermittently miss tags - symptom is a fob that works 'sometimes'.
MIFARE Classic UIDs are trivially cloneable. This is a convenience credential, not a security boundary - back it with a real lock and cameras.
parts.notes: Use the I2C variant (rc522_i2c, 0x28) if you want it on the same Grove bus as everything else; use SPI if you need faster polling. Store the tag->person mapping in Home Assistant rather than hard-coding UIDs in the device YAML, so a lost fob is revoked centrally and you are not committing access credentials into a config repo.

example.title: RC522 over I2C, forwarding scans to Home Assistant
example.source: distilled from poe-room-2-rfid.yaml - real card UIDs removed
example.code:
i2c:
  sda: GPIO16
  scl: GPIO17
  scan: true

rc522_i2c:
  address: 0x28
  update_interval: 200ms
  on_tag:
    then:
      - logger.log:
          format: "RFID tag detected: %s"
          args: ['x.c_str()']
      # Forward every scan to HA and resolve tag -> person THERE, so revoking
      # a lost fob does not mean reflashing a door node.
      - homeassistant.service:
          service: esphome.door_rfid_tag_scanned
          data:
            tag_id: !lambda 'return x;'

binary_sensor:
  # Optional: a local fast-path for one known tag.
  # Prefer the HA-side mapping above for anything you may need to revoke.
  - platform: rc522
    uid: "00-00-00-00"      # placeholder - put YOUR tag UID here
    name: "Example fob"

parts.name: MLX90614 non-contact IR thermometer (M5Stack NCIR)

i2c.how_to_change: Address is stored in on-chip EEPROM and can be rewritten, but few libraries expose it. Treat as fixed at 0x5A; use a mux for several.

parts.calibration_notes: Factory-calibrated, but like any IR sensor it reports a temperature that assumes an emissivity. Green foliage is about 0.95, not the 1.0 most libraries default to - leave it at 1.0 and leaf temperature reads low.
parts.evidence: No active config in the current fleet - canopy temperature here is measured with the MLX90640 array instead. Catalogued because it is by far the cheapest route to a leaf-temperature signal, and leaf VPD beats air VPD as a steering input.
failure_modes: Field of view is a CONE, roughly 35 degrees on the BAA. Mount it too far back and you are averaging leaf, pot, floor and lamp into one number.
Reads the first opaque surface it sees - a leaf that moves out of frame silently changes what you are measuring.
Emissivity left at 1.0 under-reads foliage by several degrees, which quietly corrupts any leaf-VPD calculation downstream.
Sensitive to its own ambient temperature; mounting it near a driver or in the lamp's radiant path biases it.
parts.notes: One spot versus the MLX90640's 768 - much cheaper, and adequate if you only need a single representative canopy point. Mount it close enough that the cone sees leaf and nothing else, and set emissivity to 0.95 before believing any number it gives you.

parts.name: MLX90640 32x24 thermal camera array

i2c.how_to_change: Address is stored in the sensor's internal EEPROM and can be rewritten, but almost nothing supports doing so. Treat it as fixed at 0x33.

parts.protocol_settings: I2C at 400 kHz minimum. 100 kHz cannot sustain a 768-pixel frame at any useful rate.

price.note: Vendor listing price for the packaged M5Stack thermal-camera unit. A bare MLX90640 breakout from a component distributor sits lower; the BAA (55 deg) and BAB (110 deg) variants also differ in price.

parts.calibration_notes: Factory-calibrated coefficients live in on-chip EEPROM; the driver reads them at boot. What you DO have to set is emissivity and reflected temperature. Green foliage is ~0.95. Leave emissivity at the default 1.0 and leaf temperature reads several degrees low, which will quietly corrupt every leaf-VPD number you calculate from it.
parts.evidence: 4 production configs run an active mlx90640 block - canopy leaf-temperature mapping in room 1 and Veg. Lower count than the CO2 fleet simply because you need one per room, not one per zone; it has been continuously deployed rather than trialled.
failure_modes: Default emissivity 1.0 under-reads leaf temperature by 2-4 C. Set 0.95 for foliage or every leaf-VPD figure downstream is wrong.
At 100 kHz I2C the frame read is too slow and you get torn or dropped frames - 400 kHz is mandatory.
The array self-heats; ta_shift exists to correct reflected temperature and the default (8 K, FLIR convention) is not always right for a sealed room.
A single hot LED driver in frame drags a whole-frame average badly - use a region of interest over the canopy, not the frame mean.
0x33 is fixed in practice, so two cameras need two buses or a mux.
parts.notes: Use a region of interest centred on the canopy rather than the frame average - the fleet configs use an 11x11 px ROI out of the 24x32 array and keep per-frame min/max as separate canopy diagnostics. Leaf temperature from this feeds leaf-VPD, which is a far better steering signal than air VPD alone.

example.title: MLX90640 tuned for canopy leaf temperature
example.code:
external_components:
  - source:
      type: git
      url: https://codeberg.org/stackdrift/esphome-components
      ref: main
      path: "."
    components: [mlx90640]

i2c:
  sda: GPIO16
  scl: GPIO17
  frequency: 400kHz     # 100kHz cannot sustain a 768-pixel frame
  scan: true

# The component DEPENDS on these platforms, so the sections must exist
# even when empty, or the build fails.
number:
select:

mlx90640:
  id: thermal_cam
  address: 0x33
  refresh_rate: "16Hz"
  resolution: "18-bit"
  pattern: "chess"
  update_interval: 20000          # ms

  # Thermography parameters tuned for plant leaves.
  emissivity: 0.95                # green foliage ~0.94-0.98. NOT 1.0.
  ta_shift: 8.0                   # reflected temp = ambient - 8C (FLIR convention)

  # Region of interest: central canopy patch. Averaging the WHOLE frame lets a
  # hot LED driver in shot drag the number - always use an ROI.
  roi:
    enabled: true
    center_row: 12
    center_col: 16
    size: 5                       # size N -> (2N+1) square

parts.name: Netafim white lateral dripline pipe (20 mm, 3 bar)
parts.protocol_settings: 20 mm OD, rated 3 bar. Takes barbed and ratchet-clip fittings.
parts.evidence: The lateral run feeding every dripper zone in this fleet. Priced per 200 m roll on the receipt, which works out around NZ$0.91 per metre.
failure_modes: White pipe is chosen to keep root-zone water cooler and to make algae visible; black pipe in a lit room heats the first shot noticeably.
Kinks at tight radii and the kink never fully recovers - it becomes a permanent flow restriction you will not find without a pressure gauge.
Barbs tear out of warm, soft pipe if the line is pressurised before the clips are on.
UV degrades LDPE over years; under direct high-intensity LED it ages faster than the datasheet's outdoor figure suggests.
parts.notes: Priced per roll, not per metre - see `unit`. The commodity fittings that go with it (barbed elbows, tees, ratchet clips, threaded tees, end caps) are all in the NZ$0.30-$4 range and are not catalogued individually; buy them as a kit with the roll. Warm the pipe end in hot water before pushing on a barb in winter.

parts.name: Netafim automatic line flush valve (16 mm)
parts.evidence: Fitted at the end of dripline runs. Opens at low pressure at the start of each irrigation and closes as the line comes up to pressure, so the line self-purges.
failure_modes: Discharges to wherever you point it - into a tray or drain, not onto the floor or into the electrics.
Fails open in grit and then bleeds continuously, which shows up as a zone that never reaches pressure.
Adds a small volume to every shot; if you are dosing precisely, account for it.
parts.notes: Solves the problem where sediment collects at the dead end of a lateral and gradually migrates back into the last few emitters. Pairs naturally with the screen filter: the filter stops most of it arriving, this clears whatever still does.

parts.name: Netafim PCJ pressure-compensating dripper
parts.subcategory: Pressure-compensating emitter with spike and tube
parts.protocol_settings: Pressure-compensating from roughly 0.5 to 4 bar. Flow rates 2 / 4 / 8 L/h depending on model.

price.unit: per dripper, incl. spike and tube

parts.evidence: The emitter behind every substrate-sensing zone in this fleet - the VWC and pore-water EC numbers those probes report are only meaningful because delivery per plant is even, which is exactly what pressure compensation buys.
failure_modes: Non-compensating drippers on a long run deliver more at the near end - the resulting VWC spread reads as sensor disagreement when it is actually a plumbing problem.
The CNL (anti-drain) variants stop siphoning between shots; without them the line drains after every irrigation and the first part of the next shot is air.
Root intrusion into the outlet on media that stays saturated.
Spikes pull out of coir under their own tube weight if the tube is not clipped - the emitter then waters the floor and the block dries out unnoticed.
parts.notes: Pressure compensation is the whole point: without it, per-plant delivery varies along the line and every substrate reading you take is comparing plants that got different amounts of water. If you are steering a crop on VWC, this is not the place to save money. Pair the anti-drain (CNL) version with the line flush valve.

parts.name: PCF8563 real-time clock
parts.subcategory: I2C real-time clock with battery backup

i2c.how_to_change: Fixed at 0x51. Rarely a problem - little else uses that address.

voltage.note: Runs down to 1.0V on backup current, so a coin cell holds time for years.

price.note: Built into most M5Stack Core and AirQ units at no extra cost.

parts.evidence: 13 configs declare an active `time: - platform: pcf8563` at 0x51, mostly the AirQ and M5 Dial units where it comes on the board. It matters because a node that loses network still needs correct local time to run a lighting or irrigation schedule.
failure_modes: Dead or missing backup cell and it silently resets to 2000-01-01 on every power cut - schedules then fire at the wrong time rather than not at all, which is worse.
Cheap modules ship with the backup-charging resistor fitted for a rechargeable LIR2032; put a non-rechargeable CR2032 in one of those and it will leak or vent.
Drifts a few seconds a day without periodic sync - pair it with SNTP and let the network correct it when available.
parts.notes: Cheap insurance for any node that runs a schedule. Configure SNTP as the primary time source and the PCF8563 as the fallback, so the node keeps sane time through a network outage and re-syncs when the network returns.

example.title: RTC as fallback, SNTP as primary
example.code:
i2c:
  id: bus_a
  sda: GPIO16
  scl: GPIO17

time:
  # Primary: network time whenever the node can reach it.
  - platform: sntp
    id: sntp_time
    servers:
      - 0.pool.ntp.org
      - 1.pool.ntp.org
    on_time_sync:
      then:
        # Push the good time back into the RTC so the coin cell holds it.
        - pcf8563.write_time:
            id: rtc_time

  # Fallback: keeps schedules honest through a network outage.
  - platform: pcf8563
    id: rtc_time
    i2c_id: bus_a
    address: 0x51
    update_interval: never

parts.name: Peristaltic dosing pump (12/24V, relay or PWM driven)

voltage.note: 12V for small dosers, 24V for the faster heads. Drive through a relay or a MOSFET, never directly from a GPIO.

price.note: Receipt price for a 24V 600 mL/min stepper-driven head bought direct from the manufacturer. Branded lab pumps of the same spec run several times this.

parts.calibration_notes: Calibrate by running the pump for a fixed time into a measuring cylinder and storing mL/s as a persistent global. Recalibrate when you change tubing - the tube IS the pump, and it work-hardens and loses volume per revolution as it ages. The deployed config stores a per-pump flow_rate global with restore_value: yes and exposes a calibration routine as a button.
parts.evidence: Four heads dosing a 200L batch tank from 50L stock tanks, in continuous production service. This is also the node the whole SAFETY pattern was hardened around - a doser that keeps running after the network drops is how you dump 50L of Core into a batch tank.
failure_modes: Tubing is a consumable. It thins, output drops silently, and your EC target quietly stops being met. Replace on a schedule, not on failure.
A stuck-on doser is the worst failure in the room. restore_mode ALWAYS_OFF plus a hard auto-shutoff delay plus ethernet on_disconnect are all mandatory - see SAFETY.md.
Dry running wrecks the head. Interlock against tank level if you can.
Back-siphoning from the batch tank into a stock tank if the head is mounted below liquid level. Mount above, or fit a check valve.
Cross-contamination between concentrated A and B parts causes precipitation in shared lines. Separate lines, always.
parts.notes: See SAFETY.md - this part is the reason that document exists.

example.title: Dosing pump with the full three-layer safety interlock
example.code:
# Three independent layers. Any one of them alone is not enough.
api:
  encryption:
    key: !secret api_encryption_key
  reboot_timeout: 5min      # LAYER 1: reboot if HA is unreachable

ethernet:
  type: IP101
  mdc_pin: GPIO23
  mdio_pin: GPIO18
  clk_mode: GPIO0_IN
  phy_addr: 1
  power_pin: GPIO5
  # LAYER 2: link drops -> everything stops, immediately, on-device
  on_disconnect:
    - switch.turn_off: motor_core_power
    - switch.turn_off: motor_bloom_power
    - script.stop: core_dose_script
    - script.stop: bloom_dose_script

globals:
  - id: core_flow_rate       # mL/s, measured by calibration run
    type: float
    restore_value: yes       # survives reboot
    initial_value: '0.0'

switch:
  - platform: gpio
    pin: GPIO26
    id: motor_core_power
    name: Core Pump
    restore_mode: ALWAYS_OFF   # LAYER 3a: never resume dosing after a power cut
    on_turn_on:
      # LAYER 3b: hardware failsafe - it cannot run longer than this,
      # no matter what the controlling automation believes.
      - delay: 600s
      - switch.turn_off: motor_core_power

parts.name: Adjustable pressure reducing valve (15-50 mm)
parts.protocol_settings: Set downstream pressure with the adjusting screw against a gauge. Typical dripline target 1.0-2.0 bar.
parts.calibration_notes: Set it against a real gauge at the far end of the run while a zone is actually flowing. Static pressure with everything closed tells you nothing useful - the number that matters is dynamic.
parts.evidence: One on the main feed. Only needed once per system rather than per zone, which is why the count is low - it is not a reflection of how well it works.
failure_modes: Set too high and pressure-compensating drippers still regulate, but every fitting and the filter housing live near their limit - failures show up at the joints, not the emitters.
Set too low and PCJ drippers drop out of their compensating range, so delivery becomes uneven again and you lose the whole benefit of buying them.
Diaphragm perishes over years and the valve drifts open, usually unnoticed until something downstream splits.
parts.notes: Mains pressure in most buildings is far above what dripline wants, and PCJ emitters only compensate up to about 4 bar. This is the part that makes the rest of the system's ratings honest. Fit a gauge downstream permanently - a NZ$20 gauge turns an invisible problem into an obvious one.

parts.name: 25 mm PVC pressure pipe (PN12)
parts.protocol_settings: 25 mm, PN12 (12 bar). Solvent-weld or threaded fittings.

price.note: The same receipt also lists a 5-length bundle at NZ$77.45, which is this per-length price times five, not a separate unit price.

parts.evidence: The rigid distribution backbone from pump to zone valves in this fleet. PVC on the pressurised mains side, LDPE lateral downstream of the valves.
failure_modes: Solvent-weld joints made in the cold or on a damp pipe fail weeks later, not immediately - which is the worst possible timing.
PN12 is comfortable for mains but the FITTINGS are usually the weak point; a pipe rated 12 bar on a 6 bar fitting is a 6 bar system.
Goes brittle under sustained UV / high-intensity LED - sleeve or paint any exposed run.
Rigid pipe transmits pump vibration into the building; use a flexible section at the pump.
parts.notes: Sold in 5.8 m lengths and often bundled - check whether a quoted price is per length or per bundle before budgeting. Commodity PVC fittings (elbows, tees, unions, valve sockets, end caps, clips) run NZ$0.79-$8 each and are not catalogued individually.

parts.name: MAX485 / SP3485 RS485-to-TTL transceiver

voltage.note: MAX485 is 5V; MAX3485/SP3485 are 3.3V. Feeding a 5V MAX485's RO pin into an ESP32 is out of spec - use a 3.3V part.

parts.evidence: Two deployments carrying the Modbus sensors. Unglamorous but it is the piece everyone forgets to order.
failure_modes: 5V MAX485 modules feed 5V into a 3.3V ESP32 RX. It usually survives and then does not. Buy the 3.3V variant.
Auto-direction modules are convenient but some clones switch too slowly at higher baud and clip the first byte of a reply. At 4800 baud you will not notice; at 115200 you will.
Missing 120R termination on a long run gives intermittent CRC errors that look like a dead sensor.
A+/B- swapped is the single most common wiring fault. Symptom is total silence, not garbage.

parts.name: Seeed LeapMMW 24 GHz mmWave presence radar
parts.protocol_settings: UART 115200 8-N-1, proprietary framed binary protocol.
parts.evidence: HALL OF SHAME. A full custom ESPHome component for this part exists in the fleet (common/sensors/leapmmw_sensor.yaml plus a 4.7 KB leapmmw_sensor.h), and ZERO of the 149 device configs include it. Someone did the integration work and then never deployed it - that is a louder verdict than any spec sheet.
failure_modes: Written and debugged, then abandoned before a single production deployment - the component is dead code.
24 GHz radar sees through thin walls and plastic, so it detects people in the NEXT room. In a compartmented facility that means constant phantom occupancy.
Oscillating fans and swaying plant canopy both register as motion - a grow room is close to the worst-case environment for this sensor.
Proprietary binary framing with sparse documentation; the custom component exists precisely because no core ESPHome driver covers it.
parts.notes: Not a bad chip, but a bad fit for a room full of moving leaves and fans. If you want presence in a grow space, a PIR outside the canopy or door contacts plus RFID will lie to you far less. Listed here so nobody else spends a weekend on the same integration.

parts.name: Senninger 20 psi fixed pressure regulator
parts.protocol_settings: Fixed 20 psi (~1.4 bar) outlet. Low-flow model - it needs a minimum flow to regulate properly.
parts.evidence: Two on zone feeds, downstream of the main reducer. Fixed-outlet regulators per zone are the cheap way to stop one zone's pressure moving when another opens.
failure_modes: Below its minimum flow it does not regulate at all and simply passes inlet pressure - a small zone on a big regulator is a silent failure.
Fixed outlet means no adjustment: buy the right psi for your emitters or buy a different one.
Directional - fitting it backwards does nothing and looks fine.
parts.notes: Per-zone regulation on top of a single main reducer keeps zones independent, so opening a second zone does not change delivery in the first. Cheap enough to fit per zone and worth it if you irrigate zones simultaneously.

parts.name: Sensirion SCD30 NDIR CO2 sensor

i2c.how_to_change: Fixed at 0x61 - which is exactly why it is useful: it does NOT collide with the SCD4x at 0x62.

parts.evidence: Not currently deployed - a common/sensors/scd30.yaml block exists in the config tree but no device includes it. Listed because its 0x61 address is the standard trick for putting two CO2 sensors on one bus without a mux.
failure_modes: Physically large and thirsty (up to 75mA peak) compared with the SCD4x.
Same ASC-in-an-enriched-room trap as the whole Sensirion NDIR family.
parts.notes: The bus-planning play: SCD41 at 0x62 plus SCD30 at 0x61 gives you two independent CO2 readings on one bus with no mux. See the I2C collision map.

parts.name: Sensirion SCD40 NDIR CO2 sensor

i2c.how_to_change: Not configurable - same fixed address as the SCD41, so they collide with each other too.

parts.calibration_notes: Same ASC caveat as the SCD41 - turn it off in an enriched room.
parts.evidence: Same silicon family and identical ESPHome config as the SCD41, one accuracy grade lower (+/-50ppm +5% vs +/-40ppm +5%). Not separately deployed here because the SCD41 was only a few dollars more.
failure_modes: Everything in the SCD41 entry applies unchanged - identical address, identical ASC trap.

parts.name: Sensirion SCD41 true NDIR CO2 sensor

i2c.how_to_change: Not configurable. Two SCD4x on one bus requires a TCA9548A mux - this is the single most common bus collision in a grow room.

parts.protocol_settings: I2C up to 100kHz. Sensirion recommend 50kHz when the Grove cable is long.

voltage.note: M5Stack Grove unit accepts 5V and regulates onboard.

price.note: Vendor listing price for the M5Stack CO2L Grove unit (the packaged form most people buy). A bare Sensirion SCD41 module from a component distributor is cheaper but needs your own cabling and enclosure.

parts.calibration_notes: Ships factory-calibrated. In a CO2-enriched room automatic self-calibration (ASC) MUST be off - ASC assumes the sensor sees 400ppm fresh air regularly, which never happens in a sealed flower room, so it will slowly recalibrate your 1500ppm setpoint down to nonsense. Do a forced recalibration in outdoor air roughly annually instead. Set altitude_compensation to your site elevation.
parts.evidence: 29 active deployments - the most-used sensor in the catalogue after the PoE board itself. It is the sensor the CO2 injection control loop actually runs on in room 1, room 2, veg and the drying room.
failure_modes: Single fixed address 0x62. Two in one room means a TCA9548A mux or two boards - plan for it before you buy the second one.
Leave ASC enabled in a sealed CO2-enriched room and it will drift your control setpoint down over weeks. This is the failure that bites people.
Self-heats. Every deployment here marks its temperature and humidity channels internal: true and reads climate off a separate SHT30.
Above roughly 2000ppm accuracy degrades; the deployed filter clamps to 300-2500ppm and drops anything outside as a bad read.
Condensation kills it. In a drying room or a room that hits dewpoint, keep it off cold surfaces.
parts.notes: The clamp-and-drop lambda below is used on all 29 deployments. Returning `{}` from an ESPHome filter lambda discards the reading entirely rather than publishing a spike - which is what you want feeding a solenoid that injects CO2.

accuracy.conditions: As published by Sensirion for the SCD41; specified across the measurement range.

example.title: SCD41 with the range clamp used on all 29 deployments
example.code:
i2c:
  sda: GPIO16
  scl: GPIO17
  scan: true
  frequency: 50kHz          # 50kHz is kinder to long Grove runs than 100kHz

sensor:
  - platform: scd4x
    address: 0x62
    update_interval: 30s
    # IMPORTANT in a CO2-enriched room: leave ASC off, or it will slowly
    # recalibrate your enriched setpoint toward 400ppm and ruin the control loop.
    automatic_self_calibration: false
    altitude_compensation: 150m
    co2:
      name: CO2
      id: co2
      filters:
        # Drop implausible readings instead of publishing a spike to the
        # controller that opens the CO2 solenoid.
        - lambda: |-
            float MIN_VALUE = 300.0;
            float MAX_VALUE = 2500.0;
            if (MIN_VALUE <= x && x <= MAX_VALUE) return x;
            else return {};
    temperature:
      name: CO2 Temperature
      internal: true          # self-heats: do not use as room temperature
    humidity:
      name: CO2 Humidity
      internal: true

parts.name: Sensirion SEN55 PM / VOC / NOx / T / RH module

i2c.how_to_change: Fixed. Collides with common IMU breakouts (MPU6050 alt address) - keep IMUs off this bus.

voltage.note: 5V supply for the fan, 3.3V logic. Do not feed it 3.3V and expect the fan to run.

parts.calibration_notes: PM is factory-calibrated. VOC and NOx are self-learning indices - give them ~12h of representative air before the numbers mean anything, and set store_baseline: true so a reboot does not restart the learning.
parts.evidence: Eight units running continuously as the per-room air-quality reference. The PM channels are the early warning for a carbon filter that has stopped filtering.
failure_modes: The fan ingests trichomes and dust. In flower it fouls fast and PM drifts high - clean annually or your baseline lies.
Self-heating makes its temperature read 1-3C above room. Mark it internal and read climate elsewhere.
VOC/NOx are indices around a learned baseline, not ppb. Do not alarm on absolute values.
