Needs a genuine 5V rail for the fan. Brown-outs show up as the fan stalling and PM flatlining rather than an error.

accuracy.spec: 0-500 index output (relative, not an absolute concentration)

example.title: SEN55 with the deployed VOC/NOx tuning
example.code:
sensor:
  - platform: sen5x
    id: sen55
    address: 0x69
    update_interval: 30s
    acceleration_mode: low
    store_baseline: true        # keep the learned VOC/NOx baseline across reboots
    pm_1_0:
      name: PM <1um
      accuracy_decimals: 2
    pm_2_5:
      name: PM <2.5um
      accuracy_decimals: 2
    pm_4_0:
      name: PM <4um
      accuracy_decimals: 2
    pm_10_0:
      name: PM <10um
      accuracy_decimals: 2
    temperature:
      name: SEN55 Temperature
      internal: true            # self-heats - not your room temperature
    humidity:
      name: SEN55 Humidity
      internal: true
    voc:
      name: VOC
      algorithm_tuning:
        index_offset: 100
        learning_time_offset_hours: 12
        learning_time_gain_hours: 12
        gating_max_duration_minutes: 180
        std_initial: 50
        gain_factor: 230
    nox:
      name: NOx
      algorithm_tuning:
        index_offset: 100
        learning_time_offset_hours: 12
        learning_time_gain_hours: 12
        gating_max_duration_minutes: 180
        std_initial: 50
        gain_factor: 230

parts.name: Sensirion SHT30 temperature & humidity sensor

i2c.how_to_change: Pull the ADDR pin high for 0x45. Gives you two per bus, which is usually enough for a room.

parts.evidence: Five deployments, all as the VPD-grade temperature and humidity reference. Accurate enough that the dehumidifier hygrostat and the VPD target run off it.
failure_modes: Two addresses only. A third on one bus needs a mux.
Prolonged high RH causes offset creep; the onboard heater clears it but adds self-heating - leave heater_enabled: false unless you are actively de-fogging.

parts.name: Sensirion SHT40 temperature & humidity sensor

i2c.how_to_change: Address is set by part variant at order time (AD1B = 0x44, BD1B = 0x45), not by a strap pin.

parts.evidence: One deployment. Successor to the SHT30 with lower power and slightly better accuracy; no reason not to use it on new builds, it just landed after the SHT30 fleet was already installed.
failure_modes: Address is fixed by part variant - you cannot strap two identical parts onto one bus.

parts.name: Shelly Pro 3EM three-phase energy meter
parts.protocol_settings: Local HTTP/RPC API plus MQTT. Integrates with Home Assistant natively - no cloud account required.

voltage.note: Mains-connected DIN-rail device. CT clamps go around the phase conductors.

parts.evidence: In service on the main distribution board here, but it is a commercial device with its own firmware rather than an ESPHome node, so it has no device config to count. Tiered on operating experience, not on config-file evidence.
failure_modes: CT clamps are directional - fitted backwards a phase reads negative, which looks like export rather than an install error.
Sized clamps: a 120 A CT on a 16 A circuit wastes most of its resolution and small loads disappear into the noise.
It is a DIN-rail mains device. Installation is an electrician's job in most jurisdictions.
WiFi in a metal distribution board is usually poor - use the wired variant or an external antenna.
parts.notes: Per-phase power is the cheapest way to catch a failing compressor, a dehumidifier stuck on, or a lighting contactor that did not drop out - all of which show up in the load curve well before anything else notices. Phase balance also matters on 3-phase supply, and this is the only thing that will tell you about it.
use_cases: equipment failure detection from load curve

parts.name: 24VAC irrigation solenoid valve

voltage.note: 24VAC is the irrigation industry standard - it is deliberately NOT DC and not mains. Needs a 24VAC transformer and a relay rated for inductive AC loads.

price.note: Receipt price for a Hunter PGV 25mm 24VAC valve. The same figure appears on two separate purchase lines, so it is a settled trade price rather than a one-off.

parts.evidence: Three zones in room 1 plus four in veg, on 1.5 minute shots. Standard irrigation hardware doing standard irrigation work - the interesting part is entirely in how you fail them safe.
failure_modes: A valve stuck open is a flooded room. This is the single highest-consequence failure in the whole catalogue - restore_mode ALWAYS_OFF plus an auto-shutoff delay is not optional.
Grit in the diaphragm holds it partly open. Fit a 130 micron filter upstream and clean it.
Inductive kickback from the coil kills cheap relays. Use a properly rated relay module or fit a snubber.
Solenoid coils buzz and get warm in normal operation - that is not a fault, but a coil that gets hot enough to smell is.
Low pressure means the diaphragm may not seat. Most valves need a minimum pressure to close reliably.
parts.notes: See SAFETY.md. Every valve in this facility carries restore_mode ALWAYS_OFF plus a 5 minute hard auto-shutoff.

parts.name: SSR-25DA solid state relay

voltage.note: 3-32 VDC control input; load side 24-380 VAC. The 3V3 GPIO of an ESP32 drives most units directly, but check yours - some clones need 4V+ to fully turn on.

price.note: Genuine Fotek costs several times a clone. Clones are commonly over-rated.

vendors.name: AliExpress SSR-25DA
vendors.note: Search the part number - individual listings rot fast

parts.evidence: Plain GPIO-driven SSRs carry the highest-current loads in the facility - CO2 solenoids, the main pump, lighting contactors and vent actuators. 8 configs switch one directly from a GPIO pin with the standard safety pattern attached.
failure_modes: Clone SSRs are routinely over-rated: a '25A' clone will cook at 10A without a substantial heatsink. Derate to about 40 percent of the badge and bolt it to metal.
SSRs fail SHORT (permanently on) far more often than open. On anything that can flood or overheat a room, put a mechanical contactor or an RCD downstream as the real safety layer.
Zero-cross types will not dim or chop a phase - do not try to use one for lighting control, use a proper 0-10V or PWM driver.
Small leakage current when off can keep neon indicators and some LED drivers faintly lit.
parts.notes: The correct pairing is: SSR switches a contactor, contactor switches the load. Driving a large inductive load straight off an SSR is how you get a welded-on output. Every SSR controlling water or CO2 in this fleet carries restore_mode ALWAYS_OFF plus an auto-shutoff delay - see SAFETY.md.

example.title: GPIO SSR driving CO2, with the dead-man timer
example.code:
switch:
  - platform: gpio
    pin: GPIO26
    id: co2_solenoid
    name: "CO2 solenoid"
    # SAFETY: never resume gas injection by itself after a power cut.
    restore_mode: ALWAYS_OFF
    # SAFETY: dead-man timer. If the controller wedges with the valve open,
    # this still closes it. Set it slightly longer than your longest real
    # injection, never "just in case" long.
    on_turn_on:
      - delay: 900s
      - switch.turn_off: co2_solenoid

parts.name: Chill Division ABD automated batch doser (STM32, hw v2.1)

vendors.name: Chill Division
vendors.note: Custom hardware - firmware source is the reference.

parts.evidence: Custom STM32 firmware for a purpose-built multi-channel batch doser, held locally as a source tree. Not currently the production doser here (that is the ESPHome peristaltic node) but it is the more capable design - deterministic timing on a microcontroller instead of a WiFi/PoE stack with a 5 minute reboot timeout.
failure_modes: Custom firmware means you own the bugs. There is no ESPHome community to fall back on.
Anything driving dosing pumps needs the same de-energise-on-comms-loss guarantee an ESPHome node gets from on_disconnect. Verify the firmware has an equivalent before trusting it.
parts.notes: Documented here for completeness because it is part of the local hardware estate. If you are building from scratch, the ESPHome peristaltic node is the lower-risk starting point.

parts.name: Submersible clean/dirty water transfer pump (750 W)
parts.subcategory: Submersible pump for tank transfer and sump duty

voltage.note: 240 VAC. Must be on an RCD - it is a mains appliance sitting in water.

vendors.name: Any hardware retailer - generic 750 W submersible

parts.evidence: One in service for tank transfer and sump duty. The receipt line carried no unit price, so this entry is band-only rather than carrying an invented figure.
failure_modes: Run dry and the seal goes in minutes - pair it with a float switch, which is the entire reason float-switch is in this catalogue.
Clean/dirty models pass solids but the impeller still jams on fibrous root material.
Not designed for continuous duty; thermal cutouts on repeated short cycles.
A mains appliance in water. RCD protection is not optional, and neither is checking the lead.
parts.notes: Transfer and sump duty only - it is not a fertigation pump and it is not rated for continuous circulation. Interlock it with a float switch so it cannot run dry, and put the same auto-shutoff pattern on it that SAFETY.md describes for valves.

parts.name: TCA9548A 8-channel I2C multiplexer

i2c.how_to_change: Three address pins A0/A1/A2 select 0x70-0x77, so eight muxes can share one bus for 64 channels. NOTE 0x70 is also the default QMP6988 address and 0x76/0x77 collide with BME280/BMP280 - check the collision map.

voltage.note: Also works as a level translator between a 3V3 master and 5V devices.

parts.evidence: 9 production configs run a TCA9548A. It exists in this fleet for exactly one reason: fixed-address parts. Two SCD4x (both 0x62) or an ENV.III QMP6988 next to a mux (both 0x70) cannot share a bus without one.
failure_modes: Its own default 0x70 collides with the QMP6988 in the M5Stack ENV.III - the most common self-inflicted collision in this catalogue. Move the mux to 0x71.
Forgetting to disable a channel leaves two channels open at once and you get corrupted reads that look like a flaky sensor.
Adds a round-trip per channel switch, so polling many sensors fast gets slow.
It does not isolate a shorted or latched-up device - one dead sensor pulling SDA low still kills its channel.
parts.notes: The single fix for an address collision. Before you buy one, check the collision map page - sometimes the cheaper answer is a second I2C bus on spare GPIO pins, which ESP32 supports natively and costs nothing.
use_cases: multiple identical sensors on one bus

example.title: Two SCD4x on one bus via a mux (moved off 0x70)
example.code:
i2c:
  id: bus_a
  sda: GPIO16
  scl: GPIO17
  scan: true

# Mux moved to 0x71: 0x70 is the QMP6988 default in the M5Stack ENV.III,
# and having both on one bus is the classic self-inflicted collision.
tca9548a:
  - address: 0x71
    i2c_id: bus_a
    id: multiplex
    channels:
      - bus_id: mux_ch0
      - bus_id: mux_ch1

sensor:
  # Both SCD4x are hard-wired to 0x62 - the mux is what makes this legal.
  - platform: scd4x
    i2c_id: mux_ch0
    address: 0x62
    co2: { name: "CO2 canopy" }

  - platform: scd4x
    i2c_id: mux_ch1
    address: 0x62
    co2: { name: "CO2 floor" }

parts.name: THC-S RS485 soil moisture / EC / temperature probe
parts.protocol_settings: Modbus RTU, typically 4800 or 9600 baud 8-N-1, default slave address 1. Registers: moisture, temperature, EC.

vendors.name: AliExpress (search THC-S RS485 soil sensor)
vendors.note: Search the part number - individual listings die constantly.

parts.calibration_notes: Factory calibration is mineral soil. A coco-coir-calibrated pore-water EC template set exists in the HAGR repo ('THC-S Home Assistant Template Sensors calibrated for Coco coir') - start there rather than from the vendor numbers.
parts.evidence: Carried over from the HAGR parts list with an existing coco-calibrated template set. Not currently wired in this facility, which went SDI-12 instead, but it is the cheapest credible substrate probe and the calibration work is already done.
failure_modes: RS485 multi-drop needs unique slave addresses set before you put two on a bus - and the address-setting tool is usually a Windows-only vendor exe.
Vendor EC compensation is for soil, not soilless. Uncorrected pwEC in coco will read low.
Quality varies wildly between sellers under the same part number.

parts.name: TP-Link Kasa KP303 three-outlet smart power strip

voltage.note: AU/NZ version is rated 240 V, 10 A and 2400 W total. Ratings and plug types differ by region; use only the local certified version.

parts.evidence: HAGR identifies the KP303 as the smart strip in use. TP-Link documents three independently controlled outlets, two always-on USB ports, 2.4 GHz WiFi and a 10 A / 2400 W total rating for the AU version. Home Assistant's official TP-Link integration explicitly lists KP303 power-strip support and uses local polling.
failure_modes: Indoor-only and not moisture rated. Do not mount it in spray, runoff, floor-level flood or heavy-condensation zones.
The current limit is shared across all three outlets. Three individually controlled sockets do not provide three times the strip's total rating.
Relays can weld closed under motors, compressors, heaters and other high-inrush loads. Use the strip for modest loads or contactor coils, not as the final safety disconnect for critical equipment.
The two USB ports are always energised and cannot be switched individually.
Newer firmware may require TP-Link account credentials for local authentication. Provision and verify Home Assistant control before depending on an automation.
parts.notes: Useful for lamps, small fans and humidifiers where three independent Home Assistant switch entities are convenient. It is not a wet-location power distribution unit, a motor contactor, or an emergency cutoff.

drivers.name: Home Assistant TP-Link Smart Home integration

parts.name: 240 V to 24 VAC 150 VA transformer
parts.subcategory: Mains-to-24 VAC supply for solenoid valves

voltage.note: 240 VAC in, 24 VAC out. 150 VA is roughly six PGV-class valves held open, or three with headroom for inrush.

parts.evidence: Every 24 VAC valve node in this fleet needs one. Counted against the configs that drive 24 VAC solenoids, since the transformer is the part that makes those work - it does not appear in the YAML itself, being upstream of the controller.
failure_modes: Undersized VA and the valves chatter instead of pulling in - size for INRUSH across every valve that can open together, not steady-state hold.
It is a mains part. It belongs in an enclosure, on its own protected circuit, wired by someone qualified to do so.
Runs warm continuously; in a sealed control box that heat has to go somewhere.
No isolation between output legs on cheap units - do not assume the 24 VAC common is at earth potential.
parts.notes: Keeping valve power at 24 VAC is the single best decision in an irrigation control box: it keeps mains out of the low-voltage enclosure entirely, so a wet fitting near the controller is a nuisance rather than a hazard. Size at roughly 3x the steady-state draw of the valves you can open simultaneously.
use_cases: keeping mains out of the control enclosure

parts.name: Tygon A-60-G chemical-resistant peristaltic tubing
parts.subcategory: Peristaltic pump tubing, chemical dispensing grade
parts.calibration_notes: Peristaltic dose volume is a function of TUBING condition, not just pump steps. Re-calibrate mL-per-revolution after fitting new tube and again once it has bedded in, or every dose you have ever calibrated is wrong.
parts.evidence: The consumable inside every dosing head in this fleet. Specified for chemical dispensing rather than generic silicone, which matters because concentrated nutrient and pH adjusters destroy the wrong polymer.
failure_modes: THE wear item in any peristaltic doser. It flattens where the rollers run and delivered volume drifts DOWN silently - your EC creeps off target and the pump reports success throughout.
Concentrated pH-down (nitric or phosphoric) embrittles cheap silicone in weeks; A-60-G is specified for it, generic tubing is not.
Replacing it changes the calibration, so a tube swap without re-calibration is itself a dosing error.
Sized bore only - the wrong ID either will not seat in the rollers or slips and pumps nothing.
parts.notes: Budget this as a scheduled consumable, not a spare part. Put a recurring reminder against it and re-calibrate on replacement. The failure mode that hurts is not a burst tube, which is obvious - it is the slow decline in delivered volume, which looks exactly like your nutrient recipe being wrong.

parts.name: Ultrasonic distance sensor for tank level

i2c.how_to_change: Only applies to I2C variants (the sonic_i2c external component). The common JSN-SR04T is trigger/echo GPIO, not I2C.

price.note: Buy the waterproof-transducer version. The bare HC-SR04 does not survive a tank headspace.

parts.calibration_notes: Measure the sensor-face-to-empty-floor distance and the sensor-face-to-full distance, then map linearly. Do it with the actual tank - nominal tank volumes are optimistic.
parts.evidence: Three deployments reading the 200L batch tank. Non-contact is the right call for a nutrient tank - nothing to foul, nothing to clean.
failure_modes: Condensation on the transducer face in a sealed tank headspace gives wild readings. Angle it or fit a shield.
Foam on the surface of an aerated nutrient tank absorbs the ping - it reads empty when it is full. This is the failure that matters.
Narrow tanks produce sidewall echoes. Mount central, keep the cone clear.
Speed of sound is temperature dependent - about 0.17% per C. In a tank room that swings 10C, that is real.
Minimum range is typically 20-25cm. Mount too low and a full tank reads as garbage.

parts.name: W5500 SPI Ethernet module
parts.evidence: Two deployments, both on boards where the Ethernet is an SPI add-on rather than a native PHY. Works, but the native-PHY PoE route is the one that scaled to 48 nodes here.
failure_modes: Uses 5 GPIO (clk/mosi/miso/cs/int) plus reset. On a crowded board that is most of your free pins.
SPI Ethernet is slower and more CPU-hungry than a native RMII PHY - noticeable if the node also drives a display.
Cheap clones ship with a duplicate or blank MAC; set one explicitly if you run more than one.

example.title: W5500 over SPI
example.code:
ethernet:
  type: W5500
  clk_pin: GPIO42
  mosi_pin: GPIO43
  miso_pin: GPIO44
  cs_pin: GPIO41
  interrupt_pin: GPIO2
  reset_pin: GPIO1

parts.name: WT32-ETH01 (ESP32 + LAN8720 Ethernet)

voltage.note: No PoE - needs a local 5V supply alongside the Ethernet run.

vendors.name: AliExpress (search WT32-ETH01)
vendors.note: Generic listings rot constantly - search the part number, do not trust any single listing.

parts.evidence: Not deployed here - the facility standardised on PoE instead. Listed because it is the cheapest way to get a wired ESP32 when you already have power at the device and only need data over the cable.
failure_modes: No PoE means two runs to every device. In a grow room that is the whole reason PoE won.
LAN8720 needs clk_mode GPIO0_OUT on most clones and GPIO0_IN on others - the boards are not consistent.
GPIO availability is poor; several pins are consumed by the PHY.

parts.name: ZPHS01B all-in-one air quality module
parts.subcategory: Multi-gas module: CO2, PM2.5, VOC, O3, CO, NO2, T/RH
parts.protocol_settings: UART 9600 8-N-1, Winsen framed protocol with checksum byte.
parts.evidence: HALL OF SHAME. A 3.8 KB common/sensors/zphs01b.yaml block exists and is referenced from the AirQ sensor library, yet no device config actually instantiates it. Worse, the lambdas in that block return an empty optional `{}` on the paths that matter, so even if you did include it, several channels would publish nothing at all.
failure_modes: The shipped lambdas return `{}` (no value) rather than a reading - the integration was never finished.
Bundling seven sensors behind one UART means one dead channel and you are replacing the whole 180 NZD module.
The electrochemical O3/CO/NO2 cells have a 2-3 year service life and drift badly; they are not calibratable in the field.
Its CO2 channel is a cheap NDIR that a single SCD41 comfortably beats for a third of the price.
parts.notes: The all-in-one temptation. In practice a SEN55 for particulates/VOC plus an SCD41 for CO2 costs about the same, is properly supported in ESPHome core, and lets you replace one sensor without binning the other. Buy the two discrete parts.

recipes.name: Budget tent monitor
recipes.summary: The cheapest honest environment monitor for a single tent: CO2, temperature, humidity and a photoperiod check, on WiFi. No actuation - this build only watches. Add relays once you trust the readings.

items.role: Host controller. Grove port feeds the whole I2C chain.
CO2 plus a usable temperature and humidity reading.
Confirms the light actually came on and at roughly the right level.

recipes.notes: Both sensors sit on one Grove I2C chain (SCD41 at 0x62, BH1750 at 0x23) with no address conflict, so this needs no multiplexer. Power the Atom from a decent 5V supply - the SCD41 pulls ~205 mA in bursts and a weak USB brick causes resets that look like sensor faults. Do NOT rely on the SCD41 temperature alone for VPD in a tight tent; it self-heats. Trim it with an offset against a reference thermometer first.
recipes.watch_out: WiFi is fine for a monitor-only build. The moment you add a valve or a heater to this, move to wired Ethernet and read SAFETY.md first - a dropped WiFi link with an open valve is how tents flood.

recipes.name: Canopy multi-sensor node (CO2 + T/RH + light)
recipes.summary: The workhorse sensing node: CO2, temperature, humidity, pressure and light on one PoE-powered I2C chain, publishing VPD, PPFD and DLI computed on the device rather than in Home Assistant. This is a real production config, not a worked example.

items.role: Host and wired network. Sensing this useful should not depend on WiFi.
CO2. Its own T/RH channels are read but deliberately not published.
The T/RH that actually gets published, plus the pressure the SCD41 is compensated against.
Lux, converted to PPFD through a two-point calibration and integrated to DLI.

recipes.notes: I2C map is clean: SCD41 0x62, SHT30 0x44, QMP6988 0x70, BH1750 0x23. No multiplexer needed. Note the ENV.III occupies two addresses - if you later add a TCA9548A it defaults to 0x70 and will collide with the QMP6988, so move the mux to 0x71.
recipes.watch_out: Four things in this config are load-bearing and are the reason it is worth copying rather than writing from scratch. First, every raw reading is cached into a global and the published sensors read the cache, so a single missed I2C read does not flap the entity to UNKNOWN and poison your history. Second, the SCD41's own temperature and humidity are read but marked internal and never published - the CO2 measurement self-heats the package, so the ENV.III is the honest source and publishing both would give you two disagreeing numbers for the same room. Third, ASC is off and forced recalibration is a button with a settable reference, because automatic self-calibration assumes weekly exposure to 400 ppm fresh air, which never happens in a sealed enriched room. Fourth, the SCD41 is pressure-compensated from the QMP6988 on the same board, which is free accuracy most builds leave on the table.

example.title: Cached readings, pressure-compensated CO2, and lux to PPFD to DLI
example.source: distilled from a production canopy node (credentials scrubbed)
example.code:
# Wired PoE node. The full config is long; this is the part that matters.
ethernet:
  type: IP101
  mdc_pin: GPIO23
  mdio_pin: GPIO18
  clk_mode: GPIO0_IN
  phy_addr: 1
  power_pin: GPIO5

i2c:
  id: bus_a
  sda: 16
  scl: 17
  scan: true

# Last-known-good cache. Published sensors read these rather than the
# hardware, so one missed I2C read does not flap an entity to UNKNOWN.
globals:
  - id: last_co2
    type: float
    initial_value: 'NAN'
  - id: last_env3_temp
    type: float
    initial_value: 'NAN'
  - id: last_env3_rh
    type: float
    initial_value: 'NAN'
  - id: last_env3_pressure
    type: float
    initial_value: 'NAN'
  - id: last_lux
    type: float
    initial_value: 'NAN'

sensor:
  - platform: scd4x
    id: scd41
    # ASC assumes weekly exposure to 400ppm fresh air. In a sealed enriched
    # room that never happens, so it must be off and recalibrated manually.
    automatic_self_calibration: false
    ambient_pressure_compensation_source: ambient_pressure_mbar
    update_interval: 30s
    co2:
      id: co2_raw
      internal: true
      on_value:
        then:
          - globals.set: { id: last_co2, value: !lambda "return x;" }
    temperature:
      id: scd41_temp_raw
      internal: true    # self-heated - read, never published
    humidity:
      id: scd41_rh_raw
      internal: true    # ditto - the ENV.III is the honest source

  - platform: sht3xd          # ENV.III half one
    i2c_id: bus_a
    address: 0x44
    update_interval: 30s
    temperature:
      id: env3_temp_raw
      internal: true
      filters: [ offset: 0.0 ]        # trim against a reference thermometer
      on_value:
        then:
          - globals.set: { id: last_env3_temp, value: !lambda "return x;" }
    humidity:
      id: env3_rh_raw
      internal: true
      filters:
        - offset: 0.0
        - clamp: { min_value: 0, max_value: 100 }
      on_value:
        then:
          - globals.set: { id: last_env3_rh, value: !lambda "return x;" }

  - platform: qmp6988         # ENV.III half two - 0x70, watch for mux clash
    i2c_id: bus_a
    address: 0x70
    update_interval: 30s
    pressure:
      id: env3_pressure_raw
      internal: true
      on_value:
        then:
          - globals.set: { id: last_env3_pressure, value: !lambda "return x;" }

  # Feeds the SCD41's pressure compensation. Free accuracy, usually skipped.
  - platform: template
    id: ambient_pressure_mbar
    internal: true
    unit_of_measurement: "hPa"
    accuracy_decimals: 0
    lambda: |-
      float p = id(last_env3_pressure);
      if (isnan(p)) return NAN;
      if (p < 800) p = 800;
      if (p > 1100) p = 1100;
      return roundf(p);

  - platform: bh1750
    i2c_id: bus_a
    address: 0x23
    id: lux_raw
    internal: true
    update_interval: 10s
    on_value:
      then:
        - globals.set: { id: last_lux, value: !lambda "return x;" }

  # ---- Published: exactly ONE temperature and ONE humidity ----
  - platform: template
    name: "Temperature"
    device_class: temperature
    state_class: measurement
    unit_of_measurement: "°C"
    accuracy_decimals: 2
    lambda: "return id(last_env3_temp);"

  - platform: template
    name: "Humidity"
    device_class: humidity
    state_class: measurement
    unit_of_measurement: "%"
    accuracy_decimals: 1
    lambda: "return id(last_env3_rh);"

  - platform: template
    name: "CO2"
    device_class: carbon_dioxide
    state_class: measurement
    unit_of_measurement: "ppm"
    accuracy_decimals: 0
    lambda: "return id(last_co2);"

  # VPD computed on the device, so it survives a Home Assistant restart.
  - platform: template
    name: "VPD"
    state_class: measurement
    unit_of_measurement: "kPa"
    accuracy_decimals: 2
    lambda: |-
      float t = id(last_env3_temp);
      float rh = id(last_env3_rh);
      if (isnan(t) || isnan(rh)) return NAN;
      float svp = 0.61078 * exp((17.27 * t) / (t + 237.3));
      return svp * (1.0 - (rh / 100.0));

  # Lux is NOT PPFD. Two-point fit against a real quantum sensor under YOUR
  # fixtures; without that this number is meaningless across spectra.
  - platform: template
    id: ppfd_calibrated
    internal: true
    lambda: |-
      float lux = id(last_lux);
      if (isnan(lux)) return NAN;
      float lux1 = id(lux_cal_1).state,  ppfd1 = id(ppfd_cal_1).state;
      float lux2 = id(lux_cal_2).state,  ppfd2 = id(ppfd_cal_2).state;
      if (lux1 <= 0 || lux2 <= 0 || lux1 == lux2) return NAN;
      float m = (ppfd2 - ppfd1) / (lux2 - lux1);
      float ppfd = m * lux + (ppfd1 - m * lux1);
      return ppfd < 0 ? 0 : ppfd;

  - platform: integration
    name: "PPFD Integral"
    id: ppfd_integral_umol
    sensor: ppfd_calibrated
    time_unit: s
    accuracy_decimals: 0

  - platform: template
    name: "DLI"
    state_class: total_increasing
    unit_of_measurement: "mol/m²/day"
    accuracy_decimals: 2
    lambda: |-
      float umol = id(ppfd_integral_umol).state;
      if (isnan(umol)) return NAN;
      return umol / 1000000.0f;

button:
  # Forced recalibration against a settable reference, since ASC is off.
  - platform: template
    name: "SCD41 Forced Recalibration"
    on_press:
      then:
        - scd4x.perform_forced_calibration:
            id: scd41
            value: !lambda "return (uint16_t) id(scd41_frc_ppm).state;"

recipes.name: Standalone CO2 injection controller
recipes.summary: Two CO2 tank solenoids on GPIO-driven SSRs, with the tightest dead-man timer in this catalogue. CO2 is the one output where a stuck-on failure is a life-safety problem rather than a crop problem, and this config is written accordingly.

items.role: One cylinder regulator, flowmeter and normally-closed injection solenoid per tank.
One per CO2 tank solenoid, driven straight off a GPIO.
Host. Any ESP32 with two spare GPIOs will do.
The CO2 reading the injection logic runs against, on a separate node or this one.

recipes.notes: The injection logic itself lives in Home Assistant; this node's job is to execute switch commands safely and to fail closed when it cannot hear from anyone. Keep the setpoint logic off the device and the safety on it.
recipes.watch_out: The auto-shutoff here is 60 seconds, not the 20 minutes used on irrigation valves, and that difference is the entire point. An irrigation valve stuck open floods a room. A CO2 solenoid stuck open displaces oxygen in a sealed space that people walk into. Sixty seconds is longer than any single legitimate injection burst and short enough that a wedged controller cannot fill the room. This node also de-energises both solenoids on WiFi disconnect rather than using a grace timer, which is the opposite of the irrigation advice in SAFETY.md and is deliberate: a brief network blip interrupting an injection burst costs you nothing, because the next burst simply resumes. None of this replaces a CO2 alarm and an interlock on the room's occupancy.

example.title: Two solenoids, 60-second dead-man, de-energise on disconnect
example.source: distilled from a production CO2 node (credentials scrubbed)
example.code:
esp32:
  board: esp32-s3-devkitc-1
  framework:
    type: arduino

api:
  encryption:
    key: !secret api_encryption_key
  # SAFETY: if Home Assistant is unreachable this long, reboot - and
  # restore_mode ALWAYS_OFF below then guarantees both tanks come back shut.
  reboot_timeout: 5min

wifi:
  ssid: !secret wifi_ssid
  password: !secret wifi_password
  # SAFETY: no grace timer here, unlike irrigation. Losing the network
  # mid-injection costs nothing - the next burst resumes. Leaving a CO2
  # solenoid open with nobody listening is a different kind of problem.
  on_disconnect:
    - switch.turn_off: tank_1
    - switch.turn_off: tank_2

switch:
  - platform: gpio
    pin: GPIO2
    id: tank_1
    name: "CO2 Tank 1"
    # SAFETY: never resume gas injection by itself after a power cut.
    restore_mode: ALWAYS_OFF
    # SAFETY: 60s dead-man. Longer than any legitimate burst, short enough
    # that a wedged controller cannot fill an occupied room.
    on_turn_on:
      - delay: 60s
      - switch.turn_off: tank_1

  - platform: gpio
    pin: GPIO1
    id: tank_2
    name: "CO2 Tank 2"
    restore_mode: ALWAYS_OFF
    on_turn_on:
      - delay: 60s
      - switch.turn_off: tank_2

  - platform: restart
    name: "Restart"

recipes.name: Full canopy stack — light, thermal, CO2, T/RH and substrate
recipes.summary: Everything needed to steer a room properly: canopy climate and CO2, real leaf temperature from a thermal array rather than an air proxy, light as PPFD and DLI, and substrate VWC and pore-water EC. This is the combination that makes leaf VPD and dryback tracking possible at the same time, which is what the commercial platforms are actually selling.
recipes.estimated_build_time: a day per room, plus calibration
recipes.network: Wired Ethernet (PoE) for the climate and thermal nodes

items.role: One host for the climate node, one for the thermal camera.
CO2 for injection control and ventilation interlock.
Published temperature and humidity, plus pressure compensation for the SCD41.
Light level, calibrated to PPFD and integrated to DLI.
Canopy leaf temperature. The reason this stack beats an air-VPD-only build.
SDI-12 host for the substrate probes.
Substrate VWC, pore-water EC and root-zone temperature.

recipes.notes: Why leaf temperature changes the picture: air VPD tells you what the air is doing, leaf VPD tells you what the plant is doing, and under high-intensity LEDs those two numbers diverge - leaf can sit below air temperature under transpiration, or above it when stomata close. Steering on air VPD alone means steering on a proxy. The MLX90640 gives a real leaf surface temperature, and combined with the ENV.III T/RH you get leaf VPD rather than air VPD. The substrate probes then close the loop: leaf VPD tells you what the plant wants to transpire, dryback tells you whether it can.
recipes.watch_out: Set MLX90640 emissivity to 0.95 for foliage. Leaving it at the 1.0 default under-reads leaf temperature by several degrees, and every leaf-VPD number downstream inherits that error silently. Use a region of interest over the canopy rather than the frame average, or a hot LED driver in shot drags the whole number. Run the thermal camera's I2C bus at 400kHz - 100kHz cannot sustain a 768-pixel frame and you get torn frames that look like sensor noise. On the substrate side, raw SDI-12 counts are not VWC: the conversion polynomial is media-specific and the coco curve is wrong for rockwool. Calibrate against gravimetric samples from your own substrate before steering anything on those numbers.

example.title: MLX90640 tuned for leaf temperature, with leaf VPD from the same node
example.source: distilled from a production thermal node (credentials scrubbed)
example.code:
external_components:
  - source:
      type: git
      url: https://codeberg.org/stackdrift/esphome-components
      ref: main
      path: "."
    components: [mlx90640]

i2c:
  sda: GPIO16
  scl: GPIO17
  frequency: 400kHz     # 100kHz cannot sustain a 768-pixel frame
  scan: true

# The component DEPENDS on these platforms, so they must exist even empty.
number:
select:

mlx90640:
  id: thermal_cam
  address: 0x33
  refresh_rate: "16Hz"
  resolution: "18-bit"
  pattern: "chess"
  update_interval: 20000            # ms

  emissivity: 0.95                  # foliage. NOT the 1.0 default.
  ta_shift: 8.0                     # reflected temp = ambient - 8C

  # Central canopy patch, not the whole frame - otherwise a hot driver
  # in shot drags the average and you steer on the luminaire.
  roi:
    enabled: true
    center_row: 12
    center_col: 16
    size: 5                         # size N -> (2N+1) square

  temperature_sensors:
    roi_avg:
      name: "Leaf Temperature"
      id: leaf_temperature
      filters:
        - median: { window_size: 5, send_every: 1, send_first_at: 1 }
    roi_min: { name: "Leaf Temperature Min" }
    roi_max: { name: "Leaf Temperature Max" }
    avg:     { name: "Canopy Average Temperature" }
    max:     { name: "Canopy Max Temperature" }

sensor:
  # Leaf VPD: saturation vapour pressure at LEAF temperature against the
  # actual vapour pressure of the air. This is the number worth steering on.
  # Air temperature and RH are imported from the climate node.
  - platform: homeassistant
    id: air_temp
    entity_id: sensor.canopy_node_temperature
    internal: true
  - platform: homeassistant
    id: air_rh
    entity_id: sensor.canopy_node_humidity
    internal: true

  - platform: template
    name: "Leaf VPD"
    state_class: measurement
    unit_of_measurement: "kPa"
    accuracy_decimals: 2
    lambda: |-
      float tl = id(leaf_temperature).state;   // leaf surface
      float ta = id(air_temp).state;           // air
      float rh = id(air_rh).state;
      if (isnan(tl) || isnan(ta) || isnan(rh)) return NAN;
      // SVP at the leaf, actual VP from the air.
      float svp_leaf = 0.61078 * exp((17.27 * tl) / (tl + 237.3));
      float svp_air  = 0.61078 * exp((17.27 * ta) / (ta + 237.3));
      float vp_air   = svp_air * (rh / 100.0);
      float vpd = svp_leaf - vp_air;
      return vpd < 0 ? 0 : vpd;

recipes.name: PoE room controller (irrigation + CO2)
recipes.summary: The pattern the reference facility flower rooms actually run: a wired PoE node that both senses and actuates, with the flood-safety pattern mandatory on every output. This is the build that can move water, so it is the build that has to fail safe.

items.role: Host + wired network. 48 nodes in production run this exact pin map.
Four irrigation zone valves, or three valves plus a CO2 solenoid.
CO2 for injection control, plus room T/RH.
Zone valves. 24 VAC keeps mains out of the control enclosure.
CO2 solenoid or a contactor coil, driven straight off a GPIO.
Keeps the irrigation schedule honest through a network outage.

recipes.notes: I2C map for this build is clean: SCD41 at 0x62, 4Relay at 0x26, RTC at 0x51. No multiplexer needed. If you add an M5Stack ENV.III you introduce a QMP6988 at 0x70 - still fine here, but check the collision map before adding a TCA9548A, which also defaults to 0x70. Note the 4Relay channel numbering is REVERSED: `relay4:` is physical relay 1.
recipes.watch_out: MANDATORY on every output in this build, no exceptions: (1) restore_mode ALWAYS_OFF so a power cut never resumes a feed, (2) an on_turn_on auto-shutoff delay sized just above your longest real feed, (3) a network killguard script with a grace timer - NOT an instant kill on on_disconnect, because brief Ethernet flaps are normal and an instant kill interrupts live feeds. See SAFETY.md for the full pattern and why each part exists.

recipes.name: Multi-zone substrate sensing array
recipes.summary: Per-zone VWC, pore-water EC and root-zone temperature over SDI-12 - the data crop steering actually runs on. One node per row, several probes per bus.
recipes.estimated_build_time: 2-3 hours per node plus probe placement

items.role: Host per row. The whole SDI-12 fleet runs this board.
Reference-grade substrate probe. The one to trust when they disagree.
Cheap SDI-12 probe. Needs a media-specific VWC curve to be usable.
Commercial SDI-12 probe, three deployed on this fleet.

recipes.notes: SDI-12 is the whole point: it is 1200 baud 7-E-1 half-duplex on a single data line, so several probes share one wire, each on its own SDI-12 address (0, 1, 2 ...). Set addresses ONE AT A TIME with a single probe on the bus, or you will address the wrong device and spend an afternoon confused. ESPHome needs two external components for this - ssieb's half-duplex uart fork and his sdi12 component - because neither is in core.
recipes.watch_out: Raw VWC counts are NOT volumetric water content. The fleet configs apply a cubic calibration polynomial to convert raw to theta, and that polynomial is specific to the medium - the coco-coir curve is wrong for rockwool and very wrong for peat. Calibrate against gravimetric samples from YOUR substrate before you steer anything on these numbers. Probe placement matters more than probe brand: same depth, same distance from an emitter, same position in the block, every zone. Inconsistent placement produces zone-to-zone differences that are pure artefact.
